chapters.title: 0. Getting Started
chapters.prerequisite: An Ubuntu computer or WSL2 console, sudo access and a tested public release. For a public server, also prepare your domain and DNS.
chapters.outcome: You know which installation path to follow and how configuration, service data and recovery fit together.
chapters.markdown:
## Your first platform, step by step

The **Bootstrapper** runs your platform. The **Wizard** configures it in your browser. **Sync** connects the two. You do not need Kubernetes experience.

1. [Install the platform](#docs/installation). Use local HTTP on a trusted Ubuntu/WSL2 computer, or choose the public-server HTTPS path.
2. [Connect and configure](#docs/configuration). Open **Wizard**, choose the pencil beside **Connect**, enter your own Sync address and credentials, then **Submit → Synchronize → Fetch**.
3. Review the settings, keep a private **Backup**, then **Push**. Push applies the configuration and restarts services automatically.
4. [Set up a runner](#docs/runners), then [create your first project](#docs/projects). Wait for its build and deployment jobs before opening its domain.

> **Tip:** Start with local HTTP to learn the workflow. Use the full public-server guide before exposing services to the internet.

## Keep two kinds of backup

**Open / Backup** and **Fetch / Push** manage configuration, including secrets. **Harvest / Seed** protects persistent service data. A configuration ZIP does not contain GitLab databases or repositories. See [Recovery](#docs/recovery) before relying on a backup.

## Check your starting point

Run this in your Ubuntu console:

```bash
uname -m
git --version
```

The public release targets `x86_64` / `linux/amd64`. The installation chapter includes Git and Docker preparation, exact release inputs, credential discovery and the expected checks at each stage.

> **Info:** Example domains and release placeholders belong to your own deployment. A standalone Wizard does not start Sync, GitLab or runners.

chapters.title: 1. Installation · local Ubuntu / WSL2
chapters.markdown:
## 0. Getting Started

This is the **local Ubuntu / WSL2 HTTP** installation. Keep it on a trusted local
computer; do not expose this unencrypted setup as a public service. You do not
need Kubernetes experience. Run commands in Ubuntu, then configure the platform
in your browser. Native Ubuntu users can skip the Windows installation step.

The **Bootstrapper** starts and manages the services. The **Wizard** is its
React interface. The **Sync service** connects the interface to the Bootstrapper
instance. GitLab, the registry and runners are added after configuration.

### 0.1 Open Ubuntu and check out the project

On Windows, open an Ubuntu WSL2 console. If Ubuntu is not installed yet, first
run this command in PowerShell:

```powershell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
```

Follow the installation steps and restart Windows if prompted. Then open Ubuntu.
Run all subsequent shell commands in the **Ubuntu console**, rather than PowerShell.

Choose a tested public release and record its exact System source revision,
complete controller digest and matching Wizard digest from the publisher's
trusted release evidence. These are operator inputs: replace the placeholders
below with that release's values. Public Docker Hub pulls do not require an
account. The declared release targets `linux/amd64`.

Install Git and check out that exact release, including its Wizard submodule:

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git
SYSTEM_REVISION='REPLACE_WITH_40_CHARACTER_RELEASE_COMMIT'
git clone https://github.com/kihyoun/system.git
cd system
git checkout --detach "$SYSTEM_REVISION"
git submodule update --init --recursive
CONTROLLER_RELEASE='docker.io/your-namespace/system@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_64_HEX_DIGEST'
WIZARD_RELEASE='docker.io/your-namespace/wizard@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_64_HEX_DIGEST'
```

The screenshots illustrate a local setup. The interface runs as a container
image: updating the Git checkout alone does not update that image. The release
installer verifies source/image identities and pulls the tested images; it does
not compile the controller or Wizard on the new host. See
[public release selection](../Prepare-Host.md#install-a-tested-public-release)
for the difference between a complete controller and a runtime base.

### 0.2 Prepare Docker and local hostnames

Install the required Docker tools:

```bash
sudo bash bootstrapper/install.sh
```

The installer installs Docker and Compose and checks Docker using a test
container. For the local HTTP test, also configure the local hostnames and the
registry's HTTP exception:

```bash
sudo bash bootstrapper/prepare-local.sh
```

WSL may regenerate `/etc/hosts` at startup. If the registry or other local
hostnames later stop resolving, run this preparation step again. It reloads the
Docker configuration without restarting the containers. The HTTP exception
remains limited to the local test.

This guide uses HTTP exclusively for local testing. A publicly accessible
instance requires its own domain and HTTPS configuration.

The controller and Wizard were built and tested in the publisher's pipeline.
Their source remains available in this checkout for inspection and development;
first installation does not run their Dockerfiles or resolve Alpine APK packages.
Building a changed version remains a separate reviewed development operation.

### 0.3 Start the Bootstrapper for the first time

Fresh Ubuntu/WSL installations use local working data at
`/var/lib/system-bootstrapper/platform` on the system disk. No second disk, USB
stick, cloud volume or Seed backup is needed for first startup. Keep WSL data
inside its Linux filesystem, rather than on a Windows-mounted path such as
`/mnt/c`, so Unix ownership and filesystem behavior are available.

Create a root-owned storage selector shared by the release installer and
lifecycle tools. This example selects the default local working directory:

```bash
sudo install -d -m 0700 /etc/system-bootstrapper
sudo tee /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env >/dev/null <<'EOF'
PERSISTENCE_MODE=local
PERSISTENT_MOUNT=/
PERSISTENT_DIR=/var/lib/system-bootstrapper/platform
EOF
sudo chmod 0600 /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
```

The native lifecycle also supports default local storage without a selector;
this walkthrough uses an explicit one. Existing selectors with
`PERSISTENT_MOUNT` and no mode retain volume semantics; they never
fall back to local storage when a required volume is absent. See the
[persistence guide](PERSISTENT_VOLUME.md) before changing an existing layout.
Configure independent backup storage when you want to Harvest or restore a Seed.
Normal operation and certificate renewal do not require that backup medium.

Then run this command from the project's root directory:

```bash
sudo env GITLAB_SSH_BIND=127.0.0.1:2222 GITLAB_REGISTRY_BIND=127.0.0.1:5050 \
  python3 bootstrapper/install-release.py \
  --controller "$CONTROLLER_RELEASE" --wizard "$WIZARD_RELEASE" \
  --persistence-env /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
```

The installer requires clean source matching the controller release and its
pinned Wizard commit. It refuses existing GitLab data or saved main configuration;
use the replacement/recovery procedure for an existing installation. It records
the selected public images in the private working configuration directory and
starts with builds disabled. Later normal startup reuses that release profile;
explicit image selectors in saved main configuration take precedence.

The Bootstrapper initially starts the Wizard and Sync access point. GitLab is not
fully configured at this stage. Image downloads and later GitLab initialization
still take time; a public release removes the source build, not service startup.

Check the containers and view the startup output with:

```bash
sudo docker ps
sudo docker logs system_bootstrapper_1
```

**Keep an Ubuntu console open under WSL** while using the platform. A running
systemd service alone does not keep the WSL instance alive.

### 0.4 Find the signature, server address and actual credentials

The original System Cube and listening address appear in the Bootstrapper output:

```text
server listening on http://<internal-container-ip>:8071
Sync authentication is configured.
```

Credentials are not printed in the logs. At first startup, generated credentials
are saved privately in `PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/sync-auth.env`. Once a main
configuration exists, its `SYNC_USER` and `SYNC_PASS` override those initial values.

Run this command locally on your own Docker host to display only the active Sync
username and password. It uses the same precedence as startup:

```bash
sudo bash -c '
  set -euo pipefail
  PERSISTENT_DIR=/var/lib/system-bootstrapper/platform
  if [[ -f /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env ]]; then
    source /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
  fi
  source "$PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/sync-auth.env"
  if [[ -f "$PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/.docker.env" ]]; then
    source "$PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/.docker.env"
  fi
  printf "Username: %s\nPassword: %s\n" "$SYNC_USER" "$SYNC_PASS"
'
```

Use the printed values in the connection dialog. Keep this terminal output
private. If you selected a custom `PERSISTENCE_ENV_FILE` at startup, use that
selector file in the command instead. Screenshots and placeholders do not
supply valid credentials for your installation.

The displayed container IP and port `8071` are the internal Node address. During
local first startup, access Sync from the browser at **`http://localhost/sync`**.
NGINX forwards this address to the Node service. The internal IP may change
whenever the container restarts.

### 0.5 Open the Wizard in your browser

Open [http://localhost/](http://localhost/).

The **Overview** opens with the project introduction, **Getting Started**
instructions and links to the handbook. Choose **Open Wizard** or the top **Wizard** tab to reach the
configuration workspace shown below. Switching between Overview, Wizard and
the footer's legal pages preserves your connection and unsent form values;
reloading the browser resets that local state.

![Getting Started overview with entry points to the Wizard and handbook](images/getting-started/00-overview.png)

If an older version is already open, reload the page. Use **Ctrl+F5** if the
interface looks outdated; the browser cache may still contain the previous version.

![Wizard before connecting: the pencil icon and Connect button are at the top right](images/getting-started/01-wizard-start.png)

Before loading a configuration, the form may contain Example values. This does
not mean GitLab has already been configured at those addresses. Do not click
Push or Seed yet.

### 0.6 Open Edit and enter the connection details first

Click the **pencil icon immediately to the left of Connect**. It opens the
**Connect** dialog with three input fields.

![Edit dialog showing Server Address and empty Username and Password fields](images/getting-started/03-edit-connection.png)

Enter the following:

| Field in the Edit dialog | Source of the value |
| --- | --- |
| **Server Address** | For this local first startup: `http://localhost/sync` |
| **Username** | The active Sync username displayed by the private local command in section 0.4 |
| **Password** | The active Sync password displayed by the same command |

**These credentials come from your own persistent configuration.** They are
separate from GitLab credentials. Do not copy them from the screenshot.

### 0.7 Connect after entering all three fields

Confirm the dialog with **Submit** after filling in all three fields. This
button signs you in; you do not need to click Connect again afterwards.

The Connect button in the main window is a shortcut using the connection settings
already stored there. Use the Edit dialog described above for your first login.

![Connected successfully: the server address, Disconnect and Synchronize are visible](images/getting-started/04-connected.png)

The server address, green dot, changed **Disconnect** button color and additional
**Synchronize** menu indicate a successful connection to the Bootstrapper instance.

### 0.8 Load the configuration with Fetch

Open **Synchronize** and select **Fetch**.

![Synchronize menu with the Fetch entry](images/getting-started/05-fetch-menu.png)

There are two cases:

- **The instance has a saved configuration:** Fetch loads those exact settings
  and the existing projects into the Wizard.
- **No main configuration has been transferred yet:** the current version requests
  derived suggestions from the connected Bootstrapper and loads them into the form.

![First startup after Fetch: suggested local hostnames marked with asterisks](images/getting-started/06-derived-settings.png)

An **asterisk** marks a derived value. Hover over it or focus it with the Tab key.
Its tooltip explains the source and asks you to verify the value before transfer.

![Asterisk tooltip explaining that derived data must be verified](images/getting-started/07-derived-tooltip.png)

Existing NGINX routes take priority when deriving suggestions. Otherwise,
hostnames may be suggested from the connection address. Suggestions do not set
up DNS or prove that a certificate exists. Unknown values remain empty;
passwords and runner tokens are not guessed.

Fetch does not write a new configuration to the server, but it replaces values
in your browser form. Use Backup first if you need to preserve unsent changes.

### 0.9 Complete the suggestions for the local test

Check the **Start**, **SSL**, **Sync** and **Wizard** sections under General:

| Setting | Value for this local test |
| --- | --- |
| `SEED_DIR` | Optional independent backup destination; leave empty until choosing Seed storage |
| `GITLAB_HOST` | `gitlab.localhost` |
| `GITLAB_REGISTRY_HOST` | `registry.localhost` |
| Gitlab Runners | Initially `0`; configure the runner after signing into GitLab |
| GitLab and registry under SSL | **Default, HTTP** |
| Enable Synchronization Server | Enable |
| `SYNC_HOST` | `sync.localhost` |
| `SYNC_USER` and `SYNC_PASS` | Choose and remember your own credentials for subsequent connections |
| Sync mode | **Default, HTTP** |
| Enable Wizard | Enable |
| `WIZARD_HOST` | `localhost` |
| Wizard mode | **Default, HTTP** |

The Seed path is a backup destination on the Docker host, not the live working
directory. First startup does not restore anything automatically. An external
backup target is required only during an explicit Harvest or Seed operation;
configure its mount/identity in the host selector before using it.

#### Public website and operator information

In **General → Website**, review the information displayed by the footer's
**Imprint** and **Privacy** pages. Operator name, postal address and contact email
start with the visible setup examples **Max Mustermann**, **Musterstraße 1,
12345 Musterstadt, Deutschland** and **kontakt@example.com**. These are actual
form values as well as input placeholders: replace them with your own public
details, or clear them. The public pages identify unchanged examples as such.
An explicitly cleared field stays empty; absent fields in older configurations
receive the setup examples.

![Website settings with public operator setup examples and optional privacy fields](images/getting-started/08-website-settings.png)

Optional fields provide a link to an additional privacy notice, the access-log
retention actually used by your deployment and additional privacy text. The
retention description does not change logging or rotation. All six fields are
public; do not enter passwords, tokens or other confidential information there.

**Backup**, **Open**, **Fetch** and **Push** include these settings. A successful
Push applies them through the normal platform restart, without an image rebuild
or CI pipeline. Startup writes only these six public strings to
`privacy-instance.json` on dedicated persistent storage. The Wizard reads that
publication without retrieving the authenticated Sync configuration.

### 0.10 Back up, transfer and apply the configuration

1. Select **Backup → bootstrapper.json → Download** to save the editable
   configuration, or **Backup → bootstrapper.zip** for JSON plus generated
   environment files. Both contain credentials; keep them private.
2. Select **Synchronize → Push** and confirm the transfer. This sends the Wizard
   settings to the instance and automatically restarts services after a successful
   import. The interface is temporarily unavailable while services start.
3. Wait for the interface to return, then reconnect and Fetch to verify the settings.

**Push transfers and applies settings. No separate Restart click is required.**
Open loads a previously downloaded JSON file into the Wizard; loading the file
alone does not change the server configuration.

### 0.11 Open GitLab and sign in for the first time

GitLab's first startup may take several minutes. Check its status in Ubuntu:

```bash
sudo docker ps
```

The GitLab container should eventually report `healthy`. Then open
[http://gitlab.localhost/](http://gitlab.localhost/).

The GitLab administrator username is **`root`**. For a fresh database, the
Bootstrapper generates a random initial password. An installation prepared with
a complete private configuration may instead set `GITLAB_INITIAL_ROOT_PASSWORD`
to at least 12 characters in `PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/.docker.env` before
GitLab's first startup. The Wizard has no dedicated field for this optional value.

Read the initial password locally after the first startup:

```bash
sudo docker exec system_gitlab_1 cat /etc/gitlab/bootstrapper_initial_root_password
```

This root-readable file is stored in GitLab's persistent configuration volume
and survives restarts. Sign in as `root` and keep the credentials private. The
file records the initial password; later password changes are not written back
to it. Harvest also includes it in the seed through the GitLab configuration
volume, so keep the seed private too.

An existing database is left unchanged. If it was set up without this mechanism,
no file containing an assumed login password is created retroactively. You can
check GitLab's native temporary file if it is still present:

```bash
sudo docker exec system_gitlab_1 grep 'Password:' /etc/gitlab/initial_root_password
```

GitLab may remove this native file on a container restart after 24 hours. If no
valid password is known, a targeted GitLab password reset is required. Sync
credentials are independent of the GitLab login.

### 0.12 Reconnect later and change settings

Open the Wizard again at [http://localhost/](http://localhost/). After completing
the setup above, the Sync address is **`http://sync.localhost`**, replacing the
first-startup `/sync` path.

Use the Edit dialog and the Sync credentials you chose in section 0.9. Load the
saved configuration with **Synchronize → Fetch**. You can change it, save a local
Backup, then apply it with Push (which restarts automatically).

For public use, configure your own DNS, HTTPS certificates and host certificate
renewal. Reusing a database or moving persistent storage requires the separate
[recovery procedure](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md).

chapters.title: 1.1 Choose an installation path
chapters.markdown:
# System Bootstrapper Handbook

Choose the complete installation path for your environment:

- [Local Ubuntu / WSL2 with HTTP](#0-getting-started): try the platform on your
  own computer, without public DNS or a certificate.
- [Public Ubuntu server with your domain and HTTPS](#public-server-own-domain-and-https):
  prepare DNS, issue certificates with Certbot and configure the services.
- [Replacement host from an external Seed](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md#restore-an-external-seed-into-a-fresh-local-installation):
  restore a completed backup into fresh local working storage.
- [Replacement host with a retained data volume](#replace-a-host-while-retaining-its-data-volume):
  reuse an existing installation, rather than initializing it again.
- [Measured installation and recovery times](#measured-installation-and-recovery-times):
  observed durations, their verification scopes and a repeatable measurement method.
- [Evolve a running system](#5-evolving-a-running-system): use one generation
  to build and test a reviewed successor, then promote it with a recovery path.
chapters.prerequisite: Choose fresh installation, Seed recovery or retained-volume reuse.
chapters.outcome: You select the path that matches your host and existing data.

chapters.title: 1.2 Public server · domain and HTTPS
chapters.markdown:
## Public server: own domain and HTTPS

This path installs a **fresh** platform on an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server with sudo
access, enough local disk space and a domain you control. An explicit mounted
live volume is optional. Reusing GitLab data requires the [replacement-host procedure](#replace-a-host-while-retaining-its-data-volume)
instead. Allocate memory, CPU and disk for GitLab plus the runner jobs you intend
to run; the Docker installation check does not establish that capacity.

The example uses `www.example.com` for the Wizard, `sync.example.com` for Sync,
`gitlab.example.com` for GitLab and `registry.example.com` for the registry.
Replace these names, the server address, administrator account and contact email
throughout. No service is configured on the bare `example.com` name in this
example; obtaining a certificate alone does not create routing for an alias.

### Public 1. Prepare DNS, ports and the host

Create these DNS records at your DNS provider. `203.0.113.10` is a documentation
address: use your server's real public IPv4 address.

| DNS name | Type | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `www.example.com` | A | `203.0.113.10` |
| `sync.example.com` | A | `203.0.113.10` |
| `gitlab.example.com` | A | `203.0.113.10` |
| `registry.example.com` | A | `203.0.113.10` |

Publish AAAA records only if this server actually serves these names over IPv6.
Remove stale IPv6 records before requesting certificates. Check all four names
from a computer outside the server, for example with `dig +short A NAME` and
`dig +short AAAA NAME`. They must resolve to this host; allow DNS changes to
propagate before proceeding.

Configure the **provider's external firewall** for this fresh server:

| Inbound traffic | Initial certificate issuance | Initial Wizard setup | Finished HTTPS installation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Your SSH port, normally TCP 22 | Allow from your administration address | Keep allowed | Keep allowed |
| TCP 80 | Allow publicly for HTTP-01 | Block public access | Allow publicly for redirects and HTTP-01 renewal |
| TCP 443 | Keep closed | Keep closed until HTTPS is configured | Allow publicly |
| TCP 8071, 5050 and 2222 | No public rule required | No public rule required | No public rule required for this example |

Apply the same restrictions in any host firewall. Keep your working SSH session
open while changing rules. The later SSH tunnel secures your browser connection;
it does **not** restrict the Bootstrapper's port-80 listener. The external rule
is therefore required during its temporary HTTP setup. Docker-published bridge
ports bypass UFW's ordinary INPUT rules and need separate attention.
The optional [separate SSH ports](#public-7-separate-administrative-and-gitlab-ssh)
procedure explains that boundary; this first-start example keeps GitLab SSH and
the direct registry port on loopback.

Connect with SSH and run these commands on the server:

```bash
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git certbot dnsutils openssl
certbot --version
SYSTEM_REVISION='REPLACE_WITH_40_CHARACTER_RELEASE_COMMIT'
git clone https://github.com/kihyoun/system.git
cd system
git checkout --detach "$SYSTEM_REVISION"
git submodule update --init --recursive
CONTROLLER_RELEASE='docker.io/your-namespace/system@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_64_HEX_DIGEST'
WIZARD_RELEASE='docker.io/your-namespace/wizard@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_64_HEX_DIGEST'
sudo bash bootstrapper/install.sh
```

Choose the source revision and both public image digests from one accepted
release, as described in [public release selection](../Prepare-Host.md#install-a-tested-public-release).
Do not use an untested branch, a runtime-base image or a floating `latest` tag.
The fresh host pulls the complete controller and Wizard instead of building
these images locally.

Use Certbot **2.3.0 or newer**, which supports `reconfigure`; the Ubuntu 24.04
[package provides that interface](https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/certbot).
The host integration below invokes
`/usr/bin/certbot` and `certbot.timer`, so this recipe uses the distribution
package, rather than a separate Snap installation. Do not run
`bootstrapper/prepare-local.sh`: public DNS and a trusted HTTPS registry replace
its local hosts-file and insecure-registry changes.

### Public 2. Select working storage and install certificate integration

This fresh installation keeps live data on the server's system disk. Create an
explicit selector so the certificate integration and lifecycle tools share the
same working directory:

```bash
sudo install -d -m 0700 /etc/system-bootstrapper
sudo tee /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env >/dev/null <<'EOF'
PERSISTENCE_MODE=local
PERSISTENT_MOUNT=/
PERSISTENT_DIR=/var/lib/system-bootstrapper/platform
EOF
sudo chmod 0600 /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
sudo bash bootstrapper/install-volume-host.sh
sudo systemctl stop certbot.timer
```

Despite its compatibility name, `install-volume-host.sh` supports local storage.
It validates working storage, connects `/etc/letsencrypt` to
`PERSISTENT_DIR/host/letsencrypt`, and installs the `system-certbot` lock wrapper
and certificate deploy hook. It does not add a Docker or renewal dependency on
an external Seed target. Reconcile conflicting active Certbot trees rather than
deleting certificate state. The timer is temporarily stopped while changing the
renewal method below.

For a deliberate volume-backed live layout instead, use `PERSISTENCE_MODE=volume`
and the actual mount point/UUID from the [persistence guide](PERSISTENT_VOLUME.md).
Do not format an existing volume. A missing selected live volume blocks startup.

### Public 3. Obtain the first certificate before starting the platform

At this point **nothing may occupy host port 80**. Inspect `sudo ss -ltnp` and
resolve any existing host web server or container deliberately. Keep public TCP
80 open for this step. Certbot's standalone server can then answer HTTP-01
without needing NGINX or a certificate first:

```bash
sudo system-certbot certonly --standalone --non-interactive --agree-tos \
  --email YOUR_CONTACT_EMAIL --cert-name example.com \
  -d www.example.com -d sync.example.com \
  -d gitlab.example.com -d registry.example.com
sudo system-certbot certificates --cert-name example.com
sudo env RENEWED_LINEAGE=/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com \
  /usr/local/sbin/system-install-certificate
```

Use a real contact email. The certificate must list all four service names and
must come from the production CA, rather than a staging certificate. If issuance
fails, check DNS/AAAA records, TCP 80 reachability and an occupied port before
retrying; do not repeatedly request new certificates to diagnose routing.

`--cert-name example.com` fixes the lineage directory name; it does not add the
bare domain to the certificate. The installed deploy hook copies the certificate
and private key to `PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/live/example.com/`. The explicit command
also makes that first copy available before a proxy exists.

| Purpose | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Complete retained Certbot state | `PERSISTENT_DIR/host/letsencrypt/`, exposed on the host as `/etc/letsencrypt` |
| Host source certificate and key | `/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem` and `privkey.pem` |
| Deployed copies on the data volume | `PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/live/example.com/fullchain.pem` and `privkey.pem` |
| Paths to enter in the Wizard, inside NGINX | `/ssl/live/example.com/fullchain.pem` and `/ssl/live/example.com/privkey.pem` |

Keep the whole Certbot tree, including `archive`, account and renewal state.
Copying just its `live` symlinks is insufficient. The Wizard does not issue a
certificate, and NGINX does not read a host `/etc/letsencrypt` path directly.

### Public 4. Configure the first startup through an SSH tunnel

**Block public TCP 80 again at the provider firewall before starting the
Bootstrapper.** Keep TCP 443 closed for now. From the project directory on the
server, start the fresh installation:

```bash
sudo env GITLAB_SSH_BIND=127.0.0.1:2222 GITLAB_REGISTRY_BIND=127.0.0.1:5050 \
  python3 bootstrapper/install-release.py \
  --controller "$CONTROLLER_RELEASE" --wizard "$WIZARD_RELEASE" \
  --persistence-env /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
sudo docker ps
sudo docker logs system_bootstrapper_1
```

The installer validates the source, exact controller and matching Wizard,
pulls the public images and starts without a source build. Its fresh-install
checks reject existing GitLab data or main configuration. A public release does
not authorize changing an existing database to another GitLab version: use the
upgrade procedure for that transition. GitLab SSH stays on loopback port 2222,
so it cannot take the host's administration port. Registry clients will use its
HTTPS name on port 443; direct host port 5050 stays private.

On **your own computer**, open another terminal and keep this tunnel running:

```bash
ssh -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
  -L 127.0.0.1:8080:127.0.0.1:80 ADMIN_USER@SERVER_IP
```

Use your SSH account, server address and `-p PORT` if needed. Open
`http://localhost:8080/`, choose **Wizard**, then use the pencil/Edit dialog with
Server Address **`http://localhost:8080/sync`**. Read the generated Sync credentials
on the server using the private command in [section 0.4](#04-find-the-signature-server-address-and-actual-credentials).
Submit the connection and select **Synchronize → Fetch**. For a fresh instance,
Fetch returns suggestions: verify and replace them with this table.

| Section / Wizard field | Value for this public example |
| --- | --- |
| General → Start: `SEED_DIR` | Empty until selecting a separate Seed backup destination |
| General → Start: `GITLAB_HOST` | `gitlab.example.com` |
| General → Start: `GITLAB_REGISTRY_HOST` | `registry.example.com` |
| General → Start: Gitlab Runners / Runner authentication token | Initially `0` / empty; register after GitLab is healthy |
| General → SSL: `GITLAB_DOMAIN_MODE`, `GITLAB_REGISTRY_DOMAIN_MODE` | **SSL encrypted**, value `2`, for both |
| General → SSL: `GITLAB_SSL`, `GITLAB_REGISTRY_SSL` | `/ssl/live/example.com/fullchain.pem` for both |
| General → SSL: `GITLAB_SSL_KEY`, `GITLAB_REGISTRY_SSL_KEY` | `/ssl/live/example.com/privkey.pem` for both |
| General → Sync: Enable Synchronization Server / `SYNC_HOST` | Enable / `sync.example.com` |
| General → Sync: `SYNC_USER`, `SYNC_PASS` | Your own non-default username and strong password |
| General → Sync: `SYNC_DOMAIN_MODE` | **SSL encrypted**, value `2` |
| General → Sync: `SYNC_SSL`, `SYNC_SSL_KEY` | `/ssl/live/example.com/fullchain.pem`, `/ssl/live/example.com/privkey.pem` |
| General → Wizard: Enable Wizard / `WIZARD_HOST` | Enable / `www.example.com` |
| General → Wizard: `WIZARD_DOMAIN_MODE` | **SSL encrypted**, value `2` |
| General → Wizard: `WIZARD_SSL`, `WIZARD_SSL_KEY` | `/ssl/live/example.com/fullchain.pem`, `/ssl/live/example.com/privkey.pem` |

To redirect additional names such as `example.com` to this Wizard, configure
[canonical Wizard aliases](WIZARD_ALIASES.md). Point each alias at this proxy
and include it in the selected certificate. Aliases are explicit saved
configuration; choosing `www.example.com` alone does not create a bare-domain
redirect. Test both HTTP and HTTPS with a path and query after Push.

The fields require the **full container paths**, including `/ssl`; any path
adornment displayed beside an input is not a replacement for that prefix. Use
hostnames without a scheme in the `*_HOST` fields. The generated GitLab and
registry external URLs must be `https://gitlab.example.com` and
`https://registry.example.com`, without `:5050`. The historical
`system/.docker.env.example` contains `/live/...` paths without the `/ssl` mount
prefix; those paths are inactive in HTTP mode and must not be copied unchanged
when enabling HTTPS. Review **General → Website** and
replace the public operator examples before publishing your site.

Save **Backup → bootstrapper.json** or **bootstrapper.zip** privately, then use
**Synchronize → Push**. A successful Push applies the configuration and restarts
the platform; the temporary `/sync` tunnel endpoint stops working as configured
HTTPS routing takes over. Do not invoke Seed to perform this fresh setup.

### Public 5. Check HTTPS, then allow public traffic

Keep SSH access and the external restriction while services start. On the server:

```bash
sudo docker ps
sudo docker exec system_web_1 nginx -t
curl --resolve www.example.com:443:127.0.0.1 -I https://www.example.com/
curl --resolve gitlab.example.com:443:127.0.0.1 -I https://gitlab.example.com/users/sign_in
curl --resolve registry.example.com:443:127.0.0.1 -I https://registry.example.com/v2/
```

Wait for GitLab to report `healthy`. The Wizard must return HTTP 200, GitLab's
sign-in page must be reachable, and an unauthenticated registry request normally
returns HTTP 401 with an authentication challenge. Do not use `curl -k`: a
hostname mismatch or untrusted certificate needs correction.

Now allow **public TCP 80 and 443** at the provider and host firewalls. From your
computer, open `https://www.example.com/`. Connect the Wizard to
**`https://sync.example.com`** with the Sync credentials you saved, then Fetch and
check the saved hostnames, modes and projects. HTTP requests for the four service
names should redirect to HTTPS, while HTTP-01 challenge files remain available
on port 80. Close the temporary SSH tunnel when it is no longer needed.

Read the initial GitLab `root` password on the server using
[section 0.11](#011-open-gitlab-and-sign-in-for-the-first-time), then sign into
`https://gitlab.example.com/` and change it. For a runner, follow
[chapter 2](#2-setting-up-gitlab-runners) using the public Wizard and Sync URLs:
set the count to `1`, keep the token empty, Push, wait for registration and check
the online manager under **Admin → CI/CD → Runners**. Git clones and registry
access in this example use HTTPS; publicly enabling GitLab SSH needs a separate,
deliberate port and firewall configuration. See
[Public 7](#public-7-separate-administrative-and-gitlab-ssh) after completing HTTPS
and renewal setup.

### Public 6. Switch unattended renewal to the running proxy

Initial issuance saved **standalone** as the authenticator. Leaving that setting
unchanged would make later renewal compete with NGINX for port 80. The current
mode-2 proxy serves HTTP-01 from the shared webroot; the initial startup proxy
and ordinary HTTP mode do not provide that route for each configured host.

On the server, create a harmless probe in the actual webroot:

```bash
sudo bash -c '
  set -euo pipefail
  source /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
  chmod 0711 "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl"
  install -d -m 0755 "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/acme-http01" \
    "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/acme-http01/.well-known" \
    "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/acme-http01/.well-known/acme-challenge"
  printf "%s\n" bootstrapper-acme-check > "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/acme-http01/.well-known/acme-challenge/bootstrapper-check"
  chmod 0644 "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/acme-http01/.well-known/acme-challenge/bootstrapper-check"
'
```

Native storage preparation adds traversal permission to the mounted `/ssl` root
and creates the public ACME webroot. This probe also creates the public challenge
subdirectories and token; it leaves `ssl/live` lineage directories and private-key
modes unchanged. Do not apply a recursive permission change to the certificate tree.

From **outside** the server, request
`http://www.example.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/bootstrapper-check` and repeat
for `sync`, `gitlab` and `registry`. All four must return `bootstrapper-acme-check`
with HTTP 200, without a redirect. For example:

```bash
for name in www sync gitlab registry; do
  curl --fail --silent --show-error "http://$name.example.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/bootstrapper-check"
done
```

Repeat the same challenge probe for every configured Wizard alias. Its normal
redirect must leave the HTTP-01 challenge path reachable directly.

After the probe succeeds, run on the server:

```bash
sudo bash -c '
  set -euo pipefail
  source /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
  /usr/local/sbin/system-certbot reconfigure --cert-name example.com \
    --authenticator webroot --webroot-path "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/acme-http01"
  /usr/local/sbin/system-certbot renew --cert-name example.com --dry-run --run-deploy-hooks
  RENEWED_LINEAGE=/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com /usr/local/sbin/system-install-certificate
  cmp /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/live/example.com/fullchain.pem"
  cmp /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/live/example.com/privkey.pem"
  docker exec system_web_1 nginx -t
  curl --fail --silent --show-error --output /dev/null \
    --resolve www.example.com:443:127.0.0.1 https://www.example.com/
  rm "$PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/acme-http01/.well-known/acme-challenge/bootstrapper-check"
  systemctl enable --now certbot.timer
'
systemctl list-timers certbot.timer
```

`reconfigure` tests against the CA staging service, then saves the successful
webroot method for future renewals. `install-volume-host.sh` rebinds existing
**webroot** paths on recovery; it does not convert a standalone lineage into
webroot renewal for you. Do not finish setup if reconfiguration or the dry-run
fails. If a lock reports an active/interrupted renewal or Harvest, resolve the
owned operation rather than deleting its lock while it may still be running.

The dry-run above explicitly runs deploy hooks using the **active trusted
certificate**, not the staging certificate. The hook copies the renewed files,
runs `nginx -t` and reloads the existing proxy. Check for a hook returning a
nonzero status: Certbot can report that failure without making renewal itself
fail. Normal `nginx -t` success messages use stderr and alone do not indicate
failure. The direct installer invocation additionally checks the installed deploy
operation with the proxy running; `cmp` confirms both deployed files match the
active lineage without printing their contents. Resolve any actual hook failure
before treating renewal as ready. The block stops on a failed
command before enabling the timer. A plain `renew --dry-run` omits deploy hooks
and is not the complete deployment check. Inspect a failure with
`sudo journalctl -u certbot.service` and `/var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log`;
check the timer and served certificate expiry periodically. Keep TCP 80 and
correct DNS available for future HTTP-01 renewals. No recurring proxy shutdown
or manual certificate copy is needed after this webroot setup.

See Certbot's upstream guides for
[standalone issuance](https://eff-certbot.readthedocs.io/en/stable/using.html#standalone),
[changing renewal configuration](https://eff-certbot.readthedocs.io/en/stable/using.html#modifying-the-renewal-configuration-of-existing-certificates)
and [deploy hooks during testing](https://eff-certbot.readthedocs.io/en/stable/using.html#testing).

### Public 7. Separate administrative and GitLab SSH

This optional procedure changes an existing HTTPS installation to this layout:

| Service | Host port | Intended inbound access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ubuntu administration | TCP 2222 | Only the trusted administrator's public source address |
| GitLab SSH | TCP 22 | Public; GitLab authenticates repository users |
| HTTP and HTTPS | TCP 80 and 443 | Public, as configured above |
| Direct registry listener | `127.0.0.1:5050` | Loopback only; external registry clients use HTTPS 443 |

`ssh -p 2222 root@server.example.com` reaches the host administration account;
use your sudo account if root login is disabled. A repository URL such as
`git@gitlab.example.com:namespace/project.git` reaches GitLab on its standard
port 22. GitLab's `git` account does not provide a root administration shell.
Register repository SSH public keys with the intended GitLab user or deploy key;
host `authorized_keys` and GitLab permissions are separate. The two SSH services
also have separate host keys. Verify fingerprints independently instead of
accepting an unexpected key after the port changes.

The Bootstrapper does not configure the host's SSH daemon or firewalls. The
following OS configuration examples use the locally assigned server IPv4
`203.0.113.10` and trusted administrator source `198.51.100.25/32`; replace both.
For a server behind NAT, bind an address actually assigned to the host and adapt
the external forwarding rules. Keep the current authenticated session open and
have provider-console recovery available throughout the change.

#### Stage and test the new administrative listener

First allow TCP 2222 from the trusted source in the provider firewall and UFW,
while retaining the rule for the working administrative port. Keep the existing
80/443 rules. Use a default-deny incoming policy, with no broader allowance for
2222. If UFW is inactive, allow the working SSH path **before** enabling it;
review existing rules rather than resetting the firewall:

```bash
sudo ufw allow from 198.51.100.25/32 to any port 2222 proto tcp
sudo ufw status numbered
sudo systemctl status ssh.socket ssh.service --no-pager
sudo systemctl cat ssh.socket
sudo systemctl show ssh.service -p KillMode
sudo ss -lntp
```

Ubuntu commonly uses [SSH socket activation](https://discourse.ubuntu.com/t/sshd-now-uses-socket-based-activation-ubuntu-22-10-and-later/30189).
On Ubuntu 24.04, a generator reads `sshd_config`; earlier migrated or custom
installations may also have socket drop-ins. Inspect both the SSH configuration
and effective units. A daemon reload alone does not replace listening sockets.

In `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/`, consolidate the intended listeners with any existing
`Port`/`ListenAddress` entries. During staging, retain administration on 22 and add
only the server's explicit IPv4 on 2222:

```text
Port 22
Port 2222
ListenAddress 203.0.113.10:22
ListenAddress 203.0.113.10:2222
```

For a socket-activated installation, make its listeners agree in a local drop-in,
for example `/etc/systemd/system/ssh.socket.d/zz-bootstrapper-admin.conf`. Create
the directory if necessary and edit that file; inspect existing drop-ins and the
effective unit so a later override cannot restore unwanted listeners:

```ini
[Socket]
ListenStream=
ListenStream=203.0.113.10:22
ListenStream=203.0.113.10:2222
```

The empty assignment clears inherited listeners. Do not use a wildcard on 2222
while Docker still publishes GitLab SSH at `127.0.0.1:2222`: those binds conflict.
Keep authentication policy unchanged and validate it with `sudo sshd -t` before
applying anything. Inspect `sudo sshd -T` as well as the effective socket unit.

The following socket replacement assumes the installed SSH service reports
`KillMode=process`, which preserves established session processes when its main
daemon stops; see [systemd process handling](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.kill.html).
If it does not, use the provider console instead of assuming the SSH session
will survive. After successful configuration validation:

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl stop ssh.socket ssh.service
sudo systemctl start ssh.socket
sudo systemctl status ssh.socket --no-pager
sudo ss -lntp
```

With service-based SSH, validate the same daemon configuration and restart
`ssh.service` instead. Confirm the actual listeners before proceeding. From a
**new client connection** at the trusted source, disable connection reuse and
require key authentication:

```bash
ssh -S none -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey \
  -p 2222 root@server.example.com
```

Verify the expected host fingerprint and that the intended administration/sudo
access works. Do not remove the old listener or firewall access until this fresh
connection succeeds. Remove any broad 2222 allow rule that would defeat the
source restriction. Handle IPv6 explicitly too: this example binds administrative
SSH only on IPv4, rather than leaving an unrestricted IPv6 listener.

#### Give port 22 to GitLab and reconcile saved configuration

In the daemon configuration and socket override, remove the staged port-22
listener, leaving only `Port 2222`, `ListenAddress 203.0.113.10:2222` and the
corresponding socket listener. Retain the empty `ListenStream=` reset. Repeat
`sshd -t`, the applicable restart sequence and the fresh key-login check above.
Use `ss -lntp` to confirm **both IPv4 and IPv6 port 22 are free of host SSH**.
Then permit public TCP 22 at the provider firewall; the administration restriction
continues to apply to TCP 2222.

After reviewing access needed by any other services, the following UFW commands
express this layout's host policy. Do not reset existing rules. Remove broader
2222 allowances, including IPv6 rules; adding a source-specific allow rule does
not narrow an existing allow-from-anywhere rule. If UFW is inactive, enable it
only after the working 2222 administration path has been allowed and freshly
tested above:

```bash
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow from 198.51.100.25/32 to any port 2222 proto tcp
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose
```

Repeat the fresh administrative key login after applying the rules. Keep IPv6
policy consistent with the addresses actually served; do not add a broad IPv6
2222 allowance to this IPv4-only administration example.

In the saved `$PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/.docker.env`, change only the SSH
binding and retain the private registry binding:

```bash
export GITLAB_SSH_BIND='22'
export GITLAB_REGISTRY_BIND='127.0.0.1:5050'
```

Preserve the exact Cube/header, image pins, secrets and all other settings. A
one-time shell override does not replace saved configuration. Schedule the GitLab
restart when jobs are idle; this operation recreates its container while retaining
the same image and persistent data. From the host, run the existing entry points
inside the accepted controller:

```bash
sudo docker exec -w /system/gitlab system_bootstrapper_1 bash -e ./start.sh
sudo docker exec -w /system/nginx system_bootstrapper_1 bash -e ./start.sh reload
```

The NGINX reload regenerates HTTPS/registry upstreams if GitLab's container IP
changed. This is a configuration change, with no image build, Seed restore or
database-version migration. Wait for GitLab readiness and verify Wizard, Sync,
HTTPS and registry access again. Fetch the saved settings in an already open
Wizard before its next Push so an old form cannot restore the previous binding.

Docker-published bridge ports can bypass UFW's INPUT rules; a default incoming
deny policy does not by itself protect a published container port. Public GitLab
22 is intentional here. Keep other bindings, especially 5050, on loopback; inspect
`docker port system_gitlab_1` and test reachability externally. Preserve Docker's
firewall management: do not set its `iptables`/`ip6tables` options to false. See
[Docker and UFW](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/packet-filtering-firewalls/#docker-and-ufw)
and the [socket-unit reference](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.socket.html).

Finally, confirm host key login still uses 2222 and test repository access from
an intended GitLab user:

```bash
git ls-remote git@gitlab.example.com:namespace/project.git HEAD
```

This validates repository read access, not push permission. The
[native runtime verifier](../bootstrapper/README.md#reviewed-replacement-host-initialization)
checks the platform's other application/storage contracts; it does not replace
these SSH and firewall checks.

chapters.title: 1.3 Installation and recovery timings
chapters.markdown:
## Measured installation and recovery times

Two operator-assisted runs on **7 November 2026** used Ubuntu **26.04.1 AMD64**,
**8 vCPUs**, approximately **32 GB RAM** and a **225 GB system disk** on each
host. Both used GitLab **19.5.3**, **four Runner managers** and System source
revision `c12a00cebe27b5d7601052448480c12494b95c19` with its pinned Wizard
submodule. Live service data used `PERSISTENCE_MODE=local` on the system disk.

| Scenario | First SSH command (UTC) | Verified ready (UTC) | Elapsed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fresh installation without Seed or external disk | 18:39:13.884 | 18:50:12.231 | **10 min 58 s** (658.347 s) |
| External Seed restored into fresh local working storage | 18:57:12.746 | 19:13:35.166 | **16 min 22 s** (982.420 s) |

The fresh installation reused only domain and Runner-count settings. It had no
previous database, service data, projects or old instance credentials. Trusted
certificates were newly issued. The complete controller and matching Wizard were
pulled from tested public release images, without building them on the host.

Recovery copied and verified approximately **3.1 GB of Seed payload** into empty
internal working storage using the matching, separately saved Wizard
configuration. The Seed retained GitLab databases, repositories, registry,
secrets and certificate/renewal state. The saved controller selector was
deliberately changed to the accepted public release; other settings and
credentials were preserved. The exact retained private Wizard and an optional
historical CI helper image were recovered from the restored registry. No separate
image archives or host builds of these images were used. Backup storage was
unmounted before platform startup.

These are three distinct storage workflows:

- **Fresh initialization:** create new service state in local working storage;
  no Seed or external medium is needed.
- **Seed recovery:** validate and copy a completed backup into fresh working
  storage, then run from that local copy. Ordinary operation, configuration
  changes and certificate renewal need no attached backup medium.
- **Retained live-volume reuse:** attach the existing live data filesystem and
  resume it without copying a Seed. This separate replacement-host path was
  **not measured** in these runs.

Harvest/Seed uses separately selected backup storage for service data. Wizard
Open/Backup and Sync Push/Fetch manage configuration independently; a Seed does
not replace the matching configuration backup. See the [storage guide](PERSISTENT_VOLUME.md)
and [recovery contract](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md).

### Timing boundaries and readiness

The clock ran from the first SSH command until the declared ready point, using
UTC timestamps and elapsed seconds. Before timing, each run already had a
provisioned VM, its address and DNS, SSH authorization, internet access and the
operator's configuration inputs. Recovery additionally had an attached completed
Seed and matching configuration backup. VM provisioning, DNS propagation and
SSH-key provisioning were excluded.

Included work covered host prerequisites and Docker installation, checkout and
submodule setup, image pulls, configuration, service startup, certificate
integration and renewal verification. Operator preparation during the run,
waits and probe retries remained on the clock: an initial Runner recent-contact
assertion was retried in the fresh run, and a metadata probe was retried during
recovery. These were attended procedures, not measurements of an unattended
installer.

Fresh readiness required trusted public Wizard, GitLab and registry responses,
authenticated idle Sync, completed certificate renewal setup with a successful
dry-run, and all four current Runner managers confirmed online in GitLab.
Recovery additionally required retained-state checks, exact historical CI helper
recovery and revocation of temporary registry credentials. Public routes and
authenticated Sync had already passed at approximately **13 min 20 s** in that
run; the additional recovery checks completed at **16 min 22 s**. Historical
Runner-manager records alone did not count as current managers.

Post-readiness audits, including subsequent image/storage and final cleanup
checks, were outside these durations. Neither run started an additional full
system-test pipeline. The historical readiness scope did not assert canonical
Wizard alias redirects; include those explicitly when required by your
deployment. These observations do not establish every application or CI workload
as tested.

The two runs performed different work and checks, so they are not a controlled
A/B benchmark or a direct performance comparison. Host performance, network and
image caches, registry availability, certificate issuance, operator interaction,
data volume and selected acceptance checks all affect elapsed time. These values
are observations, not an installation-time guarantee.

### Repeat the measurement with your own inputs

1. Record the host OS/architecture, CPU, RAM, disk and storage mode, accepted
   source and image digests, GitLab version and desired Runner-manager count.
   Supply your own domains, DNS, SSH access, firewall rules and private
   configuration. For recovery, also record the completed Seed's payload size
   and identity and verify that its separate configuration backup matches.
   Select an empty live target; never overwrite a running installation to time
   a fresh setup.
2. Define the required checks before starting. On one administration computer,
   record UTC and start a monotonic stopwatch immediately before the first SSH
   command. Keep it running through operator input, waits and retries, including
   failures that are resolved within the attempt. Record each milestone's UTC
   and elapsed time privately; do not reset the clock after a failed probe.
3. For fresh initialization, follow the [public HTTPS walkthrough](#public-server-own-domain-and-https)
   using `bootstrapper/install.sh`, `bootstrapper/install-release.py` and
   `bootstrapper/install-volume-host.sh` from the reviewed release checkout.
   Use the release's immutable controller and matching Wizard image selections.
   Configure through Wizard Fetch, Backup and Push; set four managers if
   reproducing this run's count. Complete first certificate issuance and the
   documented webroot renewal/deploy-hook check with `system-certbot`.
4. For recovery, follow [external Seed restore](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md#restore-an-external-seed-into-a-fresh-local-installation),
   including native storage preparation and
   `bootstrapper/seed-operation.sh restore --check-only` before the actual
   restore with the matching configuration backup. Keep GitLab stopped until
   restore verification finishes. After the helper completes, unmount the
   backup medium before startup to reproduce this run's storage separation.
   Install host certificate integration and start through `start.sh`. The
   [native private-Wizard recovery](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md#pulling-a-restored-private-wizard-image)
   preserves its saved digest and cleans up scoped temporary registry access.
5. Check the public Wizard, GitLab and registry with trusted TLS, authenticated
   Sync Fetch and idle status, certificate renewal/deployment, and every current
   manager's online status in GitLab. The walkthrough gives routing and renewal
   commands; [runner setup](#2-setting-up-gitlab-runners) explains the shared pool
   and manager identities. For recovery, also verify retained repositories,
   registry content and the expected saved settings. Declare any additional
   managed-image or application checks and include their recovery and temporary
   credential cleanup in your ready boundary. In workflows using the
   [native runtime verifier](../bootstrapper/README.md#reviewed-replacement-host-initialization),
   supply its private API-token file to verify recent manager contact and
   `--redirect-from` when a canonical Wizard alias is required. A skipped check
   must remain marked as skipped.
6. At the last required successful check, record the ready UTC and elapsed
   seconds and stop the stopwatch. Record later audits and cleanup separately.
   Keep credentials, configuration exports, machine addresses and raw logs in
   private operator records. Publish only sanitized context, measurement
   boundaries and results. A failed or interrupted attempt is a separate result,
   not an omitted interval in a successful duration.

chapters.markdown:
# Prepare an Ubuntu host

## Install a tested public release

For an end-user installation, use a reviewed **complete controller** image and
its matching Wizard web image from public Docker Hub repositories. The controller
is built from `system/Dockerfile`, including Sync and the lifecycle tools. The
smaller runtime base built from `bootstrapper/Dockerfile` is not a bootable
controller and must not be substituted for it.

Choose a release's exact System source revision and both immutable image
references, each ending in `@sha256:...`. The publisher's release evidence binds
the source revision/tree, pinned Wizard revision and both image IDs to those
references. Use a trusted release announcement or your own successful publication
output to obtain them. A CI job artifact is not automatically a publicly
accessible download; do not make first startup depend on access to a private
GitLab instance.

Attempt tags such as `sha-<full-System-commit>-job-<candidate-job-id>` and optional
protected version tags such as `v1.2.3` make images discoverable. The candidate job
is included because its ownership label changes the image digest: a later build
of the same commit is a separate tested attempt. A published version alias is
never reassigned to another attempt. Install by the recorded digest rather
than assuming a tag, including `latest`, is immutable. Public pulls need no Docker
Hub account; anonymous rate limits and availability of Docker Hub still apply.
The declared public release targets `linux/amd64`; it does not establish ARM64
support for the complete platform.
No image contains your private main configuration, service databases or Seed.
The public release receipt binds the two project images; it does not pin every
third-party service. Review the native GitLab, Runner and NGINX image selections
for your deployment separately.

Host preparation still installs Docker Engine/Compose from Ubuntu/Docker APT
repositories. Using release images removes controller/Wizard source builds and
Alpine package resolution from the new host; it does not remove host dependencies,
GitLab's first initialization or the requirement to maintain build inputs in CI.
See the complete [local](docs/HANDBOOK.md#0-getting-started) or
[domain/HTTPS](docs/HANDBOOK.md#public-server-own-domain-and-https) walkthrough.

## Prepare host dependencies

Run the host installer from a local checkout on Ubuntu (including Ubuntu in
WSL2 with systemd enabled). It installs Docker Engine from Docker's APT
repository, Buildx and the Compose plugin, starts Docker and runs `hello-world`.
It does not upgrade unrelated operating-system packages.

```bash
SYSTEM_REVISION='REPLACE_WITH_40_CHARACTER_RELEASE_COMMIT'
git clone https://github.com/kihyoun/system.git
cd system
git checkout --detach "$SYSTEM_REVISION"
git submodule update --init --recursive
CONTROLLER_RELEASE='docker.io/your-namespace/system@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_64_HEX_DIGEST'
WIZARD_RELEASE='docker.io/your-namespace/wizard@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_64_HEX_DIGEST'
sudo bash bootstrapper/install.sh
```

The installer provides a `docker-compose` wrapper for the orchestration scripts.
It uses `docker compose --compatibility` to preserve their expected
underscore-separated container names. Service configuration, persistence and
platform acceptance are separate steps.

## Publish your own public releases

Keep source development, merge review and required candidate checks in GitLab.
Public Docker Hub publication is a distribution step after the applicable
checks; it does not make Docker Hub the development or Production control plane.
The publisher copies the exact accepted complete controller and Wizard image
identities instead of rebuilding a different image after testing.

Configure the System GitLab project's CI variables for your Docker Hub namespace:

| Variable | Value / handling |
| --- | --- |
| `DOCKERHUB_PUBLISH_ENABLED` | Protected variable; `true` opts into public release publication |
| `DOCKERHUB_REPOSITORY` | Protected variable; your public controller repository, for example `your-namespace/system` |
| `DOCKERHUB_WIZARD_REPOSITORY` | Protected variable; your public Wizard repository, for example `your-namespace/wizard` |
| `DOCKERHUB_USER` | Protected and masked publisher identity with write access to those repositories |
| `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` | Scoped write token; protected and masked, never stored in source |

Create the public repositories and configure protected default-branch/release-tag
rules before enabling publication. Keep publisher credentials unavailable to
untrusted merge-request code. The public release receipt records source and image
identities, not credentials or installation data. Share that receipt or its
source/digest selections through a public release channel if other operators
should install it; publishing container images alone does not publish private
GitLab job artifacts.

Restrict repository writes to the publication identity. Where available, enable
Docker Hub's repository-side immutable tag policy for `sha-*` and `v*` aliases.
CI serializes its publishers and refuses an already conflicting alias, but that
check cannot atomically exclude another external publisher's simultaneous push.
The recorded digest, rather than an alias, remains the installation authority.

## Local integration test

Select compatible GitLab and Runner releases explicitly. The example below uses
GitLab CE 19.5.3 and Runner 19.5.1, pinned by the security release profile and
disposable integration suite. Do not point a new major version at existing GitLab data without following
GitLab's supported upgrade path.

For the local integration setup, include these optional exports in the complete
private main configuration at `PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/.docker.env` before
starting GitLab. Do not create a partial main configuration containing only
these options. Inside the controller, `system/.docker.env` is a compatibility
link to the saved configuration; the persistent copy takes precedence over
configuration embedded in an image:

```bash
export GITLAB_IMAGE=gitlab/gitlab-ce:19.5.3-ce.0@sha256:6863d156a1a477bd6f69fc674b671d0163cd8b06bf63bb17cc4a4a803b78b27c
export GITLAB_RUNNER_IMAGE=gitlab/gitlab-runner:v19.5.1@sha256:8e049fb719162488893a9eccc48f3a05259d02f2386dfbb20f3e379a50575afd
export GITLAB_SSH_BIND=127.0.0.1:2222
export GITLAB_REGISTRY_BIND=127.0.0.1:5050
```

Use `gitlab.localhost`, `registry.localhost`, `sync.localhost` and `localhost`
as the respective GitLab, registry, sync and wizard hosts, with domain mode 0
(HTTP) and matching external URLs. Run `sudo bash bootstrapper/prepare-local.sh`
to add the local hostnames and the Docker HTTP exception for
`registry.localhost:5050`. This helper is opt-in for local tests; production
should use its configured domains and certificates. It preserves other Docker
daemon settings. The port overrides above apply to GitLab SSH and registry,
not to the platform's web listener.

For the managed local GitLab, set the runner count to 1 and leave its token blank:
the bootstrapper creates/reuses the shared pool automatically. Fetch afterwards
loads its runner token. See [the handbook](docs/HANDBOOK.md#2-setting-up-gitlab-runners).
Alternatively, create a runner in GitLab and supply its `glrt-` authentication
token as `GITLAB_RUNNER_TOKEN` with `GITLAB_RUNNER_SCALE=1`.
The registration script also accepts legacy registration tokens and verifies
existing registrations instead of duplicating them.

Copy `tests/registry/registry-smoke.gitlab-ci.yml` into a disposable GitLab project's
`.gitlab-ci.yml` to reproduce the integration test. It uses this platform's
Docker socket runner and covers a single-architecture image without
attestations. The fixture disables BuildKit attestations because affected
Docker/GitLab versions can reject their manifests with `blob unknown to registry`.
See the [GitLab compatibility workaround](https://support.gitlab.com/hc/en-us/articles/29426166749596-Push-to-Container-Registry-Fails-Error-error-from-registry-blob-unknown-to-registry).

Keep tokens and generated `.docker.env` files out of Git. Use the
[disposable integration suite](tests/e2e/README.md) for isolated platform
acceptance rather than running fixture projects against retained user data.

## Boot

A fresh installation uses local working data at
`/var/lib/system-bootstrapper/platform` on the Ubuntu/WSL system disk. No attached
volume or Seed is required. To choose the layout explicitly, create a private
host selector:

```bash
sudo install -d -m 0700 /etc/system-bootstrapper
sudo tee /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env >/dev/null <<'EOF'
PERSISTENCE_MODE=local
PERSISTENT_MOUNT=/
PERSISTENT_DIR=/var/lib/system-bootstrapper/platform
EOF
sudo chmod 0600 /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
sudo env GITLAB_SSH_BIND=127.0.0.1:2222 GITLAB_REGISTRY_BIND=127.0.0.1:5050 \
  python3 bootstrapper/install-release.py \
  --controller "$CONTROLLER_RELEASE" --wizard "$WIZARD_RELEASE" \
  --persistence-env /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
```

Use the Linux filesystem under WSL, not a Windows-mounted data directory.
Startup validates free space, permissions and filesystem behavior. Existing
`PERSISTENT_MOUNT` selectors without a mode retain their volume semantics.
For an explicit live volume, select `PERSISTENCE_MODE=volume` and its actual
mount/UUID; a missing selected volume fails closed rather than creating local
replacement data. Changing the mode never migrates an existing installation.
See [working storage and backup media](docs/PERSISTENT_VOLUME.md).

Install Certbot separately on hosts using HTTPS, then run
`sudo bash bootstrapper/install-volume-host.sh` for persistent TLS state and
renewal integration. Local mode needs no extra mount dependency. Neither Docker,
normal service startup nor certificate renewal depends on an external Seed target.

`install-release.py` verifies the clean checkout and pinned Wizard revision
against the pulled public-image identities. It refuses an existing main
configuration or GitLab data rather than treating a reinstall as an upgrade.
It records only the two release image selectors in the private
`configuration/.release-images.env` and invokes native startup with builds
disabled. Ordinary subsequent `sudo bash start.sh` calls reuse that profile;
explicit saved main-configuration selectors still take precedence. `--install-host`
can perform the Docker installation when it has not already been run. This
installer does not restore a Seed, import a configuration ZIP or issue certificates.

On a fresh local installation, open `http://localhost/` on the host. The pulled
Bootstrapper starts the configuration Wizard and Sync proxy. Allow time for
image downloads and service startup. Read the generated first-setup Sync login privately from
`PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/sync-auth.env` (mounted at `/state/sync-auth.env` in
the controller). Saved main configuration in `configuration/.docker.env` is
loaded afterwards and may override `SYNC_USER` and `SYNC_PASS`; use those saved
values when present. Startup logs do not print the password.

Under WSL, keep an Ubuntu shell open while using the platform: systemd services
alone do not keep the WSL instance alive. See
[Microsoft's WSL systemd documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/systemd).

## Seed lifecycle

### First-setup suggestions in the Wizard

`Synchronize → Fetch` first requests the saved configuration. Only a missing main
configuration (HTTP 404) triggers the authenticated `GET /config/suggestions` endpoint. Authentication and
other server errors do not trigger guesses.

Suggestions use the generated NGINX routing templates when available. Missing
service hostnames can be proposed from the connection/server hostname. These
are suggestions only: they do not verify DNS, provision domains or establish
that HTTPS is available. IP addresses, Docker-style container IDs and the
example.com/org/net placeholder domains are not used to invent hostnames.
Unknown values remain blank in the Wizard. Passwords and runner tokens are
not inferred. The user must complete and verify the form before pushing it.

The Wizard marks derived values with `*` and a tooltip asking the user to verify
them. A saved configuration always takes precedence, including values that the
user might want to change. Reading suggestions never creates or changes a
configuration, starts services, or applies a seed.

This keeps the configuration workflow (`Open` / `Backup`, `Push` / `Fetch`)
independent from the persistent-data workflow (`Harvest` / `Seed`). Configuration
is persisted separately beneath `platform/configuration` and mounted at `/state`;
suggestions themselves never save or apply configuration automatically.

After compiling sync, run `node tests/sync/config-suggestions.js`. The API test
`node tests/sync/config-suggestions-api.js` must run in a disposable container: it
starts its own sync process on port 8071 with a temporary configuration tree.

### GitLab first administrator login

The username is `root`. For a fresh database, the bootstrapper generates a unique
initial password, or accepts `GITLAB_INITIAL_ROOT_PASSWORD` (at least 12 characters)
from the complete private main configuration at
`PERSISTENT_DIR/configuration/.docker.env`. The controller reads this through
its `system/.docker.env` compatibility link; the persistent saved configuration
takes precedence over configuration embedded in an image. The tracked example
deliberately has no shared default password.

Read the password locally after startup:

```bash
sudo docker exec system_gitlab_1 cat /etc/gitlab/bootstrapper_initial_root_password
```

This root-readable file lives in the persistent GitLab configuration volume and
is retained across restarts, unlike GitLab's temporary initial-password file.
It is also included when harvesting the GitLab configuration into a seed: treat
that seed as containing credentials. Store the password privately and change it
after login. The retained file records the initial password, not later changes.
An existing file is never overwritten, and an existing PostgreSQL directory
without that file causes generation to be skipped. Setting this option does not
reset an existing GitLab account; use GitLab's password-reset procedure instead.

Sync and GitLab administrator credentials are separate. The retained password
file must not be published in a repository or diagnostic log.

Run `node tests/gitlab/root-password.js` to check the initialization behavior
using temporary directories without touching a running GitLab installation.

### Persistent state

`SEED_DIR` is an independently selected backup destination. Its optional
`SEED_MOUNT`/`SEED_UUID` identify removable storage and are checked only when
creating or reading a Seed. Local live mode requires an external backup
filesystem; legacy volume mode may keep a disjoint Seed on its retained volume. A transient operation helper binds that destination;
normal controller/GitLab containers do not retain a `/seed` mount. Harvest
creates a completed recovery snapshot containing service data from `/srv`, TLS
files from `/ssl`, and complete Certbot account/renewal state. It stops GitLab,
requires a clean exit, verifies a checksum/ownership manifest, and atomically
selects the new snapshot through `seed/current`. Earlier snapshots are retained.

Seed restore is explicit; startup does not automatically overwrite live data.
Restore requires fresh live service-data directories, GitLab absent or stopped,
a completed manifest and the same GitLab image identity. An incomplete or
legacy unmarked Seed is rejected before copying. A missing Seed leaves existing destination data alone.
Configuration remains a separate Wizard backup, and the Wizard does not download
service-data Seeds. See the [recovery contract](docs/RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md) for
locks, failure handling and restoration on empty storage.

The shell/rsync regression uses temporary data and a fixture Docker command:

```bash
python3 tests/seed/recovery-contract.py
```

Run the [full disposable acceptance suite](tests/e2e/README.md) to exercise real
GitLab, registry, runner CI, configuration export and TLS renewal together.

## Shutdown
```bash
bash stop.sh
```

chapters.prerequisite: Read Getting Started and choose an installation path.
chapters.outcome: You understand the services, state boundaries and the order of everyday configuration tasks.
chapters.markdown:
## The pieces of your platform

| Component | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Bootstrapper | Starts and coordinates containers and persistent storage |
| Wizard | Browser interface for configuration, runners and projects |
| Sync | Authenticated API between the Wizard and the Bootstrapper |
| GitLab | Source repositories, merge requests and pipelines |
| Runner managers | Execute pipeline jobs in a shared runner pool |
| Registry | Stores the container images built by pipelines |
| NGINX | Routes each configured domain to its service or environment |

## A safe configuration cycle

**Connect → Fetch → edit → Backup → Push → reconnect → Fetch.** Fetch loads saved settings, or marked suggestions on first setup. Review suggestions before transfer. Push applies settings and restarts services automatically.

> **Warning:** Backup files contain credentials. Keep them private. Configuration backups and completed service-data Seeds are separate recovery inputs.

## What survives a change

Source and images describe the infrastructure. Persistent service data contains repositories, databases, registry content and secrets. Saved configuration takes precedence over first-install examples. [Working storage](#docs/storage) explains local data, optional live volumes and independent backup media.

## Build, verify, promote

A source import installs source. A build produces a candidate. Review and Beta are optional environments. Production promotion is a separate deliberate operation with exact image evidence and a rollback checkpoint. Follow [Evolution](#docs/evolution) for the full platform and the linked Wizard guides for interface delivery.

chapters.title: 3. Configuration · main actions
chapters.markdown:
## 1. Main actions

| Action | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Edit (pencil) | Opens the dialog for the server address and Sync credentials |
| Submit / Connect | Signs the Wizard into the Sync service |
| Disconnect | Disconnects the Wizard |
| Open | Loads a configuration file from your computer into the Wizard |
| Backup | Downloads configuration as JSON or a ZIP containing JSON and generated environment files |
| Fetch | Retrieves saved instance settings; without a configuration, the current version loads marked suggestions |
| Push | Transfers the Wizard configuration and automatically restarts the instance |
| Restart | Restarts services using the transferred configuration |
| Register / Unregister | Checks/registers or unregisters configured runner managers |
| Harvest | Publishes a cold snapshot of GitLab data, certificates and certificate-renewal state in the seed directory |
| Seed | Validates a completed Seed and restores into fresh live service-data directories |
| Reset | Deletes the main and project configurations through the reset workflow |
| Update | Updates source code through the existing update workflow |

**Configuration and persistent service data are managed separately.** Open/Backup
and Push/Fetch manage configuration. Harvest/Seed handle service data. Neither
configuration download includes the Seed, databases or registry contents. Harvest
and Seed are not needed to view a configuration with Fetch.

Current implementation detail: the existing Wizard **Seed** action also
transfers the main configuration from the form before restoring data. Check the
form before invoking it. First-startup suggestions did not change this coupling.
Use Push for the initial setup in chapter 0.

Harvest stops GitLab and requires a clean shutdown before copying its data. It
coordinates with certificate renewal and publishes a checksummed completion
manifest only after copying succeeds; previous completed snapshots remain
available. Seed validates the snapshot and requires the matching GitLab image
before restoring. Save a matching configuration backup separately and follow the
[recovery contract](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md). Local live layouts require a separate external Seed filesystem. Legacy
volume layouts may keep their disjoint Seed on the retained live volume; that
does not protect against losing that volume.
