chapters.title: 3.1 Canonical Wizard aliases
chapters.markdown:
# Canonical Wizard aliases

An installation can explicitly reserve additional DNS names that permanently
redirect to its configured Wizard origin. With `WIZARD_HOST=www.example.com` and
`WIZARD_DOMAIN_MODE=2`, an alias `example.com` redirects both
`http://example.com/a?x=1` and `https://example.com/a?x=1` to
`https://www.example.com/a?x=1`. Redirects use HTTP 308 and preserve the original
path and query. The target comes from saved configuration, never the incoming
Host header. No alias is inferred from a `www` prefix.

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `WIZARD_ALIASES` | Optional space-separated exact DNS names. Empty or absent disables alias routes. |
| `WIZARD_ALIAS_SSL` | Optional certificate path inside NGINX, beneath `/ssl`. Defaults to `WIZARD_SSL`. |
| `WIZARD_ALIAS_SSL_KEY` | Optional private-key path beneath `/ssl`. Defaults to `WIZARD_SSL_KEY`. Set both overrides together. |

The Wizard must be enabled and have an exact canonical host with domain mode
`0` (HTTP target) or `2` (HTTPS target). An alias serves both HTTP and HTTPS even
when the canonical target is HTTP, so alias TLS still needs a certificate. The
selected certificate must cover **every alias** and its key must match. Configure
DNS, certificate issuance and renewal using the public-server installation
procedure before enabling aliases; this setting does not obtain certificates.
Preserve the full Certbot account and renewal tree as described in the handbook.

Names must contain valid DNS labels, with no schemes, ports, IP literals,
wildcards or trailing dots. Comparison ignores case. Duplicate aliases and a
canonical-host loop are refused. Assigned GitLab, registry and Sync names are
reserved, including applicable wildcard modes. Enabled production, beta and
review project names are reserved too, including the managed Wizard's optional
environments. A wildcard service `*.apps.example.com` reserves its subdomains;
it does not reserve `apps.example.com` itself. Empty alias configuration leaves
the installation's existing domain modes and routing contracts in place.

## Configure through the supported configuration workflow

Fetch the current saved configuration in the Wizard and download a private ZIP
backup. Extract it into a private directory, retaining `.docker.env` and
`.projects.env/` together. Use the helper from the reviewed checkout to produce
a new configuration file. Node is already included in the controller image; it
can also run the helper on a workstation with Node installed.

```sh
private_config_dir="$HOME/private-bootstrapper-config"
node nginx/wizard-aliases.js configure \
  --config "$private_config_dir/.docker.env" \
  --projects "$private_config_dir/.projects.env" \
  --alias example.com \
  --output "$private_config_dir/candidate.docker.env"
```

Repeat `--alias HOST` for each additional name. When the aliases use a different
certificate, add both `--certificate /ssl/live/aliases.example.com/fullchain.pem`
and `--key /ssl/live/aliases.example.com/privkey.pem`. Existing override settings
are retained when those arguments are omitted. To remove all redirects, use
`--clear` instead of the `--alias` arguments.

The helper validates the Cube signature, host conflicts and certificate-path
syntax before creating an exclusive mode-0600 output file. It changes only its
alias assignments, preserving the Cube and all unrelated configuration bytes.
It does not replace the input, print credentials, write live NGINX configuration
or restart services. Keep both the old configuration and the resulting file
private. Use an up-to-date complete project export so validation can account for
the installation's assigned project names.

In the Wizard, choose **Open** and select `candidate.docker.env`. Keep
`.docker.env` in the filename so Open identifies it as main configuration.
Review the canonical Wizard settings and existing projects, then choose
**Backup** to retain the updated JSON/ZIP and **Synchronize → Push** to apply it.
Fetch again before editing from another browser or an older form.

These settings use the Wizard's existing additional `runtimeOptions` support.
Fetch/Open preserves unknown main-environment keys there; JSON Backup/Open and
ZIP/Push carry them forward, including after unrelated form edits. There is no
dedicated alias form field. For an intentional JSON edit, put the values under
`main.runtimeOptions`, for example:

```json
{
  "WIZARD_ALIASES": "example.com",
  "WIZARD_ALIAS_SSL": "/ssl/live/example.com/fullchain.pem",
  "WIZARD_ALIAS_SSL_KEY": "/ssl/live/example.com/privkey.pem"
}
```

Do not substitute this fragment for a complete configuration backup. Ordinary
Push and project changes validate conflicts before changing saved configuration.
Start/reload validates the saved alias routing again before replacing templates.

## Rendering, restart and recovery

`nginx/start.sh` reconstructs `zz-wizard-aliases.conf.template` from the saved
main and project configuration on every start and reload. It overwrites that
template with empty content when aliases are disabled, so an earlier generated
route cannot survive removal. The registry-only recovery phase also clears it;
normal startup reconstructs it after the Wizard is available. No private helper
or retained template is required.

Configuration backup remains separate from service-data backup. Preserve the
updated Wizard JSON/ZIP with the matching completed Harvest/Seed. Restore both
into fresh live storage using the recovery procedure. Seed retains certificate
and service state; the separate configuration restores the alias settings. A
Seed without matching configuration is not a complete installation backup.
Normal operation does not need the backup medium attached.

## Verify a configured installation

Run the native verifier with the operator-supplied alias origin in addition to
its ordinary configured-service checks:

```sh
sudo python3 bootstrapper/verify-runtime.py check \
  --persistence-env /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env \
  --baseline "$private_config_dir/pre-start-baseline.json" \
  --output "$private_config_dir/runtime-check.json" \
  --redirect-from https://example.com
```

Use the verifier's normal baseline, checkout and credential arguments for the
operation being performed. Where the installation requires an alias, keep
`--redirect-from` in its readiness invocation. Verify HTTP as well as HTTPS,
an encoded path with a query, and public TLS trust. Repeat after repository-owned
NGINX reload, service restart and a disposable configuration-plus-Seed restore.
The bundled platform tests perform these lifecycle checks with generic test
domains and a local ACME issuer.

Both alias virtual hosts serve `/.well-known/acme-challenge/` directly from
`/ssl/acme-http01`. An existing challenge returns its content without a redirect;
a missing challenge returns 404 without a Location header. Check certificate
renewal using the documented webroot/deploy-hook procedure, including NGINX
configuration validation and reload. A redirect response alone does not prove
that certificate issuance or renewal works.

chapters.title: 4. GitLab runners
chapters.markdown:
## 2. Setting up GitLab runners

A runner executes jobs in your GitLab pipelines. It can be set up automatically
for the Bootstrapper's own GitLab instance. Automatic setup requires GitLab 16
or newer; the historical GitLab 12 image default does not support this workflow.
Use the image settings from chapter 0 for the local test.

### 2.1 Set the count and start the runners

1. Open the Wizard and connect to Sync using **Edit → Submit**.
2. Load the existing configuration with **Synchronize → Fetch** so the next Push
   preserves your configured hosts.
3. Under **Gitlab Runners**, enter the desired count, initially **1**. The allowed
   range is 0 to 50; choose a count appropriate for your computer's memory and CPU.
4. Leave **Runner authentication token** empty for automatic setup. A token
   already loaded by Fetch can stay in place: it will be reused.
5. Transfer and apply the settings with **Synchronize → Push**; restart is automatic.
   Wait for GitLab startup and runner registration.
6. Check the Ubuntu console:

   ```bash
   sudo docker ps
   ```

   With a count of 1, `runner_docker_1` should be present. A running container
   alone does not confirm successful registration. After registration, the
   Bootstrapper reports `Runner runner-docker-1 registered.`, or
   `Runner runner-docker-1 verified.` when checking an existing registration.
7. Sign into GitLab as an administrator and check **System Bootstrapper Docker
   pool** under **Admin → CI/CD → Runners**. Its connected runner managers must
   be online. Projects can use this instance runner when instance runners are
   enabled for that project.

The count means **runner containers in a shared instance runner pool**. GitLab
shows one runner entry with multiple managers, rather than a separate global
runner entry for each container. Open the runner's detail page and inspect
**Runner managers** for each container's system ID and online status. The
automatically created pool has the tags `docker` and `aws` and also accepts
untagged jobs.

### 2.2 Show the token and download the configuration

1. After restarting, reconnect the Wizard to the configured Sync address if
   needed, for example `http://sync.localhost` locally.
2. Select **Synchronize → Fetch**. The Wizard now also loads the generated runner
   token from the Bootstrapper configuration.
3. The token is hidden by default. Use **Show** to display and copy it from the
   input field; **Hide** conceals it again.
4. Select **Backup** to download the configuration, including its runner token,
   as Bootstrapper JSON. Keep this file private.

The export stores the token under `gitlabRunnerToken` and the count under
`gitlabRunnerScale`. The token belongs to that GitLab instance; an independent
new GitLab database will not recognize it. Leave the field empty again for
automatic first setup against a new database. Manually supplied tokens are also
supported and are not replaced with automatically generated ones.

### 2.3 What happens internally

The Bootstrapper waits for GitLab's readiness check and uses its existing Docker
access to its own GitLab container. Inside that container, it creates a temporary
administrator access token with the `create_runner` scope, creates the instance
runner through the GitLab API, and immediately revokes the access token, including
on API failure. The access token stays inside the GitLab process and appears in
neither the Wizard nor the JSON backup. It expires the following day as a fallback
for abrupt process termination; subsequent setup also revokes leftover setup tokens.

Only the runner authentication token is saved in the Bootstrapper configuration.
Repeated registration reuses the existing pool. Each manager persists its own
`config.toml` and system ID beneath `PERSISTENT_DIR/runners/<pool>/<index>/`.
Restarts reuse these identities. Scaling down retains the directories so a
later scale-up can reuse them; stopped managers can remain visible as offline
entries in GitLab. Do not delete the whole runner pool to remove one old manager.
Runners use the `gitlab` service name on the shared Docker network so a GitLab
restart with a different internal
IP does not break their connection. Register updates old internal IP endpoints
in managed runners without changing their tokens or externally configured addresses.
Recovery after interrupted configuration persistence locates the managed pool by
name. Keep that entry's name unchanged if you want this recovery behavior.

**Register** starts or scales runners using the saved configuration and checks
their registration. **Unregister** unregisters the managers. With modern token
registration, the global runner entry remains in GitLab. Count **0** stops the
runner containers without deleting the pool or token. Wizard changes are only
transferred when you use Push.

This setup does not change the Harvest/Seed cycle. Bootstrapper configuration
continues to be managed through Push/Fetch and Open/Backup.

### 2.4 Local functional test

For an explicitly disposable local test instance, `tests/gitlab-runner/live/runner.py` creates
a private test project and pipeline, checks the runner and downloads the generated
result file. It creates a separate temporary test access token with the `api`
scope and revokes it afterwards. This is a test helper; actual runner setup only
requires `create_runner`.

If runner setup fails, platform startup continues so you can correct the
configuration in the Wizard. Check the Bootstrapper output, correct the settings
and try **Register** again.

```bash
sudo python3 tests/gitlab-runner/live/runner.py
```

Prerequisites are running local services, Docker access, and the addresses
`gitlab.localhost` and `sync.localhost` on the local HTTP proxy.

chapters.markdown:
# Runner persistence

`start.sh` reads the platform's `PERSISTENT_DIR` and generates a Compose service
for each runner manager. Manager `runner_docker_1` binds:

- `PERSISTENT_DIR/runners/runner/1/config` to `/etc/gitlab-runner`;
- `PERSISTENT_DIR/runners/runner/1/home` to `/home/gitlab-runner`.

Project pools use `runners/<project>_runner/<index>/` instead. Each manager keeps
its own `config.toml`, runner system ID and home. The runner image's declared
volumes therefore do not create anonymous storage. Do not scale the template
service directly: its bind mounts cannot distinguish individual managers.

Each pool uses one GitLab runner record and authentication token. Its managers
have distinct system IDs; GitLab lists them under the runner's **Runner managers**
section rather than as separate runner records. Saved per-manager configuration
keeps those identities stable across restarts.

Counts from zero through 50 are supported. Shrinking removes the excess
containers while retaining their directories; growing reuses those directories.
`stop.sh` also retains registration and data. Run `unregister.sh` explicitly only
when intentionally removing registration. The generated Compose file is
temporary; its paths are deterministic and reconstructed on each invocation.

When invoking these scripts inside the bootstrapper, mount the host's
`PERSISTENT_DIR` at the same absolute path inside the container. Runner directories
are prepared there before the host Docker daemon mounts them. The platform must
check that the persistent volume is mounted before startup. A migration from
anonymous volumes must copy each existing manager's config and home into its
corresponding directory before replacing its container.

`provision.js` writes the main configuration under `SYSTEM_CONFIG_DIR` when set
(the controller uses `/state`). This preserves the legacy configuration symlink
when atomically recording a newly provisioned runner token.

Run the lifecycle regression in the built controller image too, since its
BusyBox utilities differ from the Debian component-test image. Set
`BOOTSTRAPPER_IMAGE` to the exact controller image you built:

```sh
docker run --rm --network none --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:exec \
  -v "$PWD:/work:ro" -w /work --entrypoint node \
  "$BOOTSTRAPPER_IMAGE" tests/gitlab-runner/persistence.js
```

This uses the runtime's actual `mktemp`, without Docker access or live state.

chapters.outcome: Runner managers retain their individual identities across container recreation and scale changes.

chapters.title: 5. Projects and environments
chapters.markdown:
## 3. Configuring applications and environments

The Wizard's **Projects** section was previously named **Proxy**. It describes an
application with its **Production**, **Beta** and **Review Apps** environments.
Use **Add Project** to create its deployment configuration. An NGINX proxy forwards
requests for configured domains to the corresponding application containers.
The proxy is one part of the application configuration.

Some images in chapter 0 still show the former **Proxy** label. The current
interface uses **Projects** in the same location.

For new projects, the **Project Key** is exactly the GitLab name and path. Only
lowercase letters a–z and digits are allowed; existing stored keys are not renamed.

Connect the Wizard to Sync and use **Fetch** first. Under **Projects → Add Project**,
choose the namespace, check availability and configure the enabled environments
with their HTTP/HTTPS settings. **Save** creates a private GitLab repository with
a README and generated CI. Setup reports progress asynchronously. Occupied
repositories are neither adopted nor overwritten; repeated Save does not create
duplicates.

### 3.1 Start an application from a template

In the creation dialog, choose an **Application template**:

| Selection | Generated starter |
| --- | --- |
| React + TypeScript + Vite | React source, Vite build, lockfile and Dockerfile |
| Angular + TypeScript | Angular source, CLI build, lockfile and Dockerfile |
| General web project | HTML, CSS and JavaScript without a framework build, with a Dockerfile |
| Empty repository | Repository and CI only; add your own source later |

The first three options include a Dockerfile. Save creates the files and matching
CI and starts the first pipeline after configuring routing. The pipeline builds
and publishes the image, checks its HTTP response and starts automatic deployments.
For a manual deployment, start the corresponding job in GitLab yourself.

Open the pipeline link and wait for the build and deployment jobs to succeed
before checking the application domain. A repository link alone does not prove
that an application is running. You can then work directly on the generated
source; the Dockerfile and pipeline remain editable too. GETTING_STARTED.md in
the new repository explains the local commands. New Angular and React projects
build with Node 24, as does the System Wizard itself.

An empty repository is not yet a running application. In that workflow, the
pipeline waits for application source with a Dockerfile. Repository metadata
survives Fetch and JSON Backup/Open. See the [project guide](PROJECT_BOOTSTRAP_GUIDE.md)
for the complete instructions, including recovery after errors.

### 3.2 The automatically registered System Wizard

After the platform has a main configuration and GitLab is available, startup
automatically registers **wizard** as the first project when the Wizard is
enabled. Use Fetch after registration completes. Its Production URL, HTTP/HTTPS
mode and certificate paths come from the actual Wizard settings under General;
locally, the existing interface remains at `http://localhost`.

The project starts with a private `root/wizard` repository scaffold containing
README and managed CI. Expand its row and select **Initialize Wizard source**
to preview and explicitly import the pinned application source. See the
[source initialization guide](WIZARD_SOURCE.md) for preparation and safe retry.
This source-only action does not start a pipeline or deploy another interface.
After initialization, **Build and verify Wizard** opens a separate read-only
preview. **Enable build pipeline** explicitly installs the managed recipe and
starts or recovers its initial pipeline. See the [build workflow guide](WIZARD_BUILD.md)
for required matching versions, verified candidate evidence and safe recovery.
Build activation does not deploy the candidate. Optional Review and Beta
environments require explicit configuration and manual GitLab deployment jobs;
Production promotion uses its separate guarded operator workflow. The existing
Wizard container and Production route are reused, with no duplicate project proxy.
Manage the interface settings under General; the system project is read-only in
the project list. Its repository links and configuration survive Fetch, Backup,
Open, Push and restart. Repeated startup reuses the same repository.

If a local `wizard` key or an unrelated GitLab repository already exists, the
Bootstrapper reports the conflict without overwriting it. A registration failure
does not replace or stop the working interface. Check the Bootstrapper output,
resolve the reported conflict/readiness problem and restart to retry.

#### Build and check the Wizard manually

Before starting, use matching System and Wizard versions that expose the source
and build actions. The System image must contain its prepared pinned Wizard
source package. GitLab, its project registry and a shared runner accepting the
`docker` tag must be available. The runner needs the reviewed Docker executor
setup used by the managed recipe, including Docker/Buildx access and registry
connectivity. Confirm sufficient physical disk and RAM for the build; avoid
running competing infrastructure builds at the same time. New imports use the
pinned Node 24/React 19/Vite 8 source and matching modern build recipe. Existing
legacy imports require the explicit [upgrade procedure](../project-bootstrap/wizard-upgrade/README.md);
reimporting source is not an upgrade mechanism.

For the local WSL setup, run `sudo bash bootstrapper/prepare-local.sh` again
after a WSL restart if `registry.localhost` no longer resolves. WSL can regenerate
`/etc/hosts`. The preparation reloads Docker configuration without restarting
the running containers; retry the failed job in the same pipeline afterwards.

1. Open the existing Wizard address. Use the pencil icon beside **Connect** to
   enter the configured Sync address and your current Sync credentials, then
   choose **Submit**. After first setup, use the configured Sync domain rather
   than assuming the initial `http://localhost/sync` path is still correct.
2. Select **Synchronize → Fetch**. In **Projects**, expand the first **wizard**
   entry. Check its repository link and the existing Production address. If the
   managed entry is missing, resolve registration first; do not create a second
   Wizard project with **Add Project**.
3. If source is already initialized, retain its receipt and skip to step 4;
   do not reimport after managed build activation. Otherwise choose
   **Initialize Wizard source**. Check the preview's **Repository**,
   **Source revision** and **Files**, then choose **Import source**. Wait for
   completion. This imports the source pinned by this System version without
   starting a pipeline. If source was already imported, retain that receipt;
   reimporting is not a source-upgrade mechanism.
4. Close the source dialog and choose **Build and verify Wizard**. Check the
   **Repository**, **Imported commit** and **Recipe version**. The preview alone
   does not create a pipeline or change the repository.
5. Choose **Enable build pipeline** once. Wait for the controller operation to
   finish; it records the managed recipe and initial pipeline. An interrupted
   browser response is a reason to inspect/refresh the saved operation, not to
   delete its receipt or create another project.
6. Choose **Open pipeline** in the build dialog. In GitLab, inspect the same
   pipeline's `build:wizard` and `test:wizard` jobs. The first runs the
   pinned application checks and production build, then publishes a candidate
   image. The second pulls the immutable image and checks HTTP, rendered UI, Projects and SPA
   navigation in an isolated browser candidate. A pending runner or running job
   has not passed these checks.
7. Return to the Wizard and choose **Refresh status** after the jobs finish.
   Wait for **Candidate checks and the immutable artifact are verified** and
   **Verified candidate image**. Record the pipeline and the image reference
   ending in `@sha256:…`. A green pipeline alone does not replace the controller's
   required-job and matching-artifact verification.
8. Inspect the GitLab job artifacts if evidence is needed: `build-evidence.json`
   from `build:wizard`, and `wizard-evidence.json` plus `browser-evidence/` from
   `test:wizard`. Evidence belongs to that pipeline and commit. The recipe
   currently retains these artifacts for seven days; an expired artifact may
   prevent a later verification even when an earlier job was green.
9. Confirm the existing Wizard still opens at its original address. Fetch again
   and check that the same project/repository and Production address remain.
   Build verification does not replace the running interface. To deploy the
   candidate, configure the [managed Review and Beta environments](../project-bootstrap/wizard-environments/README.md)
   and use their manual GitLab jobs. Production promotion and rollback use the
   separate [guarded operator procedure](../project-bootstrap/wizard-production/README.md).

For failures, use the [build status and recovery table](WIZARD_BUILD.md#status-and-safe-continuation).
Retry failed jobs in the same GitLab pipeline, then refresh status. Resume only
when the dialog offers **Resume activation**, after **Refresh preview** confirms
the current state. **Pipeline creation has an uncertain outcome. Refresh only.** permits refresh
only and needs administrator inspection; never clear its durable checkpoint to
force another pipeline. Keep credentials out of screenshots, issue comments and
job-log excerpts.

### 3.3 Shared and additional runners

The runner settings have two different purposes:

| Location in the Wizard | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| General → Gitlab Runners | Shared instance runner pool available to multiple GitLab projects |
| Projects → Additional runners (optional) | Additional runner containers for this application configuration, using a separately supplied token |

Start with **0** additional project runners. Your pipelines can use the shared
pool when instance runners are enabled for the GitLab project and the job tags
match. A value of 0 does not disable the shared runners; it simply starts no
additional containers for this application.

For additional runners, their GitLab registration and token determine which
projects can use them. Associating a runner with a Project Key alone does not
restrict it to that GitLab project. Automatic token creation in chapter 2 applies
to the shared instance pool.

chapters.title: 5.1 Create an application · detailed guide
chapters.markdown:
# Creating an application project

Connect the Wizard to Sync, Fetch the saved configuration, then open
**Projects → Add Project**. Enter a nonempty Project Key containing only lowercase
ASCII letters and digits. Choose a GitLab namespace and application template,
then configure Production, Beta and Review App hosts with their HTTP/HTTPS,
certificate and deployment settings. The destination below the key is the exact
repository path; domains do not change it. Existing stored keys are not renamed.

The key field distinguishes checking, available, occupied and unverified.
A local duplicate or occupied GitLab destination blocks creation. An API failure
does not mean a name is free. Save rechecks GitLab; a competing creation is
reported without linking to it, overwriting it or adding a suffix.

## Save and inspect the first pipeline

Save creates a private repository, uses its configured default branch, installs
managed CI at `.system-bootstrapper/ci.yml` and selects that CI path. Provisioning
runs server-side through an authenticated background job; the browser polls
short requests. Keep the form open until completion. A failed request can be
retried with Save. After a browser/service restart, Fetch the pending
configuration and use **Edit → Save** to resume the same operation.

The private operation receipt is stored in `.projects.env/.<key>.env`. Conflicting
configuration/service mutations are excluded while provisioning runs. Do not
replace a pending configuration or delete its receipt to bypass recovery.

React, Angular and General web projects receive editable application source,
Dockerfile, NGINX configuration and matching CI. React uses TypeScript/Vite;
Angular uses its CLI build. Both use Node 24 with pinned dependencies and
lockfiles. General web starts with static HTML/CSS/JavaScript and needs no Node
build. `GETTING_STARTED.md` in the created repository gives local commands.

Once routing is ready, Save starts the initial pipeline. It builds and pushes an
image, performs an HTTP smoke check and deploys automatic environments. Start
manual deployment jobs in GitLab. Inspect the pipeline link for the actual
result: a queued build does not mean an application is running. Retrying Save
recovers the initial pipeline instead of starting duplicates.

An **Empty repository** contains README and generated CI, not a running
application. Add source and a root Dockerfile compatible with the generated
Docker/Cypress workflow before building or deploying. Environment URLs are
configured destinations, not health checks.

Repository ID, path, URLs, default branch, managed CI path and operation state
survive Fetch and configuration Backup/Open. Ordinary environment edits use the
configuration/Push workflow; they do not rename the repository or automatically
rewrite committed CI. Review pipeline changes in the repository explicitly.

## Manage the system Wizard project

Startup with the configured Wizard enabled registers it as the first system
project. General supplies its existing Production host and certificates, so
registration creates no second proxy for that host. Edit/delete and ordinary
environment switches are disabled for this managed entry. Repeated startup
retains the repository and its server-owned workflow metadata. Resolve a local
key or repository ownership conflict before retrying startup.

Registration alone installs a disabled scaffold. Use the managed project actions
to [initialize pinned source](WIZARD_SOURCE.md), [build and verify a candidate](WIZARD_BUILD.md)
and configure [Review/Beta environments](../project-bootstrap/wizard-environments/README.md).
The optional environments begin disabled and require explicit host/certificate
configuration. Their deploy/stop jobs are manual. A candidate replaces the
Production interface only through the separate guarded
[operator promotion procedure](../project-bootstrap/wizard-production/README.md).

Push/Fetch and Open/Backup manage configuration independently of Harvest/Seed,
which handles persistent service data and certificates. Save actual
configuration backups privately; generated source repositories are not a place
for credentials or exported configuration.

## Verification

Build Sync with `cd sync && npm run build`. The isolated API regression
`node tests/gitlab/project-bootstrap.js` uses port 8071 and must run in a
disposable container/network namespace. It covers validation, authentication,
namespace conflicts, competing Save, recovery, polling, configuration-write
exclusion and Fetch round trips. Template generation is covered by
`node tests/gitlab/application-templates.js`.

For Wizard checks, use the Node/npm versions declared in `wizard/package.json`,
install with `npm ci`, then run `npm run lint`, `npm test`, `npm run build` and
`npm run test:config-export` from the Wizard directory. Tests cover metadata,
certificate/deployment settings, key validation and ignored stale responses.

`tests/gitlab/live/project-bootstrap.js` is an opt-in test for a disposable
platform. It takes Sync credentials through the environment and a
`PROJECT_PAYLOAD` JSON file containing `{projectKey, namespaceId, data, ci}` from
the Wizard generator. It creates or resumes its `bootstrapdemo` project, checks
concurrent/repeated Save and Fetch, and leaves that project for inspection. Do
not point it at an unrelated existing key. Template live checks are in
`tests/gitlab/live/application-templates.js` and
`tests/gitlab/live/application-templates-audit.rb`.

`tests/wizard/default-wizard.js` and
`tests/nginx/default-wizard-routing.sh` cover managed registration and single-route
behavior; `tests/wizard/live/default-wizard.js` is its authenticated live check.
Local HTTP fixtures do not demonstrate real DNS, certificate issuance/renewal,
GitLab job execution or a successful Production rollout. Exercise those gates
separately on an explicitly owned test platform.

chapters.title: 5.2 Project bootstrap reference
chapters.markdown:
# Project bootstrap

Project bootstrap connects application configuration to a private GitLab
repository, managed CI, environment networks and NGINX routing. The Wizard's
**Projects → Add Project → Save** flow performs provisioning through the
authenticated Sync service. See the [operating guide](PROJECT_BOOTSTRAP_GUIDE.md)
for the browser procedure.

## Application templates

| Template | Generated application |
| --- | --- |
| React | TypeScript/Vite application, locked dependencies, Node 24 build and NGINX runtime. |
| Angular | TypeScript/Angular CLI application, locked dependencies, Node 24 build and NGINX runtime. |
| General web project | Framework-free HTML, CSS and JavaScript served by NGINX without a Node build. |
| Empty repository | README and managed CI; application source and a root Dockerfile must be supplied separately. |

Template files are versioned under `project-bootstrap/templates/`. Source,
Dockerfile, runtime configuration and CI remain editable after creation.
Generated application pipelines build an image, publish it to the instance
registry, perform an HTTP smoke check and deploy enabled environments according
to their configured automatic/manual settings. The pipeline uses
`CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH` instead of assuming a branch name.

## Repository identity and collisions

The repository display name and path are exactly the Project Key: key `mywebapp`
creates `<selected-namespace>/mywebapp`. New keys must match `^[a-z0-9]+$`.
The UI and backend reject spaces, punctuation, uppercase letters and empty keys;
they do not silently normalize input. Existing stored keys remain importable.
GitLab reserved-name or namespace-permission failures are reported separately.

Production, Beta and Review domains are independent settings. Changing a domain
does not rename the repository. An occupied destination blocks creation; the
bootstrapper does not overwrite it, silently link it or invent a suffixed name.
The saved operation identifies a successful retry of the same request.

The debounced availability check uses the complete namespace/repository path.
Duplicate local keys also block creation. Lookup failures mean unverified
availability, and stale responses are ignored after changing the key or
namespace. Save rechecks GitLab and treats the actual create response as
authoritative, including races after an earlier successful check.

## Provisioning and recovery

The Sync service reserves the local key before asynchronous provisioning and
stores the operation receipt in `.projects.env/.<key>.env`. Repository creation,
template installation and CI selection run through the instance's GitLab Rails
adapter. A temporary scoped API credential stays server-side and is revoked
when the operation ends. No GitLab administration credential reaches the
browser or configuration export.

Repository identity is saved before routing is applied. A retry can therefore
repair routing or recover the initial pipeline without creating another
repository. Polling returns completion or a safe error through authenticated
short requests. Pending operations exclude conflicting configuration/service
mutations. An unrelated repository, edited managed file or uncertain external
result must be inspected rather than bypassed by resetting its receipt.

The selected CI path is `.system-bootstrapper/ci.yml`. Upstream publishing files
are preserved separately. Environment settings and generated routing must agree
with the managed pipeline. Project provisioning keeps GitLab running.

## Managing the Wizard itself

With the Wizard enabled and configured, startup automatically registers the
private `root/wizard` system project. It represents the existing interface;
its Production host, HTTP/HTTPS mode and certificate settings come from General.
Repeated startup retains repository identity, workflow receipts and installed
optional environment settings. An occupied local key or foreign repository is
reported without being overwritten.

Registration creates a disabled README/CI scaffold. Subsequent actions are
explicit and independent:

1. [Initialize source](WIZARD_SOURCE.md) from the committed System Wizard gitlink.
2. [Build and verify](WIZARD_BUILD.md) the imported application and immutable
   registry candidate.
3. Configure [Review and Beta](../project-bootstrap/wizard-environments/README.md)
   on separate HTTPS hosts and deploy/stop them through manual GitLab jobs.
4. Apply a verified candidate with the guarded
   [Production promotion and rollback procedure](../project-bootstrap/wizard-production/README.md).

Source import, candidate builds and Review/Beta deployment do not replace the
running management interface. Production promotion is an operator-confirmed
action. Importing source does not change the upstream repository or make this
instance the development source of truth; primary/backup repository selection
is a separate [configuration decision](GITLAB_GITHUB_BACKUP.md).

## Configuration and service data

Project identity and workflow receipts survive authenticated Fetch, Backup/Open,
Push and restart. The managed Wizard entry keeps its Production settings in
General, while optional managed environments use their dedicated dialog.
Harvest/Seed handles service data and certificates; configuration backup remains
separate. Keep secrets out of repository files and retained build evidence.
chapters.prerequisite: A configured GitLab instance and Sync connection; choose a new unoccupied repository identity.
chapters.outcome: You understand template provisioning, retry behavior, ownership and the separate Wizard workflow.

chapters.title: 6. Operations · host maintenance
chapters.markdown:
## Optional weekly host maintenance from a trusted Codex host

An operator can authorize a trusted, always-on administration host to run the
following Ubuntu maintenance procedure weekly. Codex is optional; the platform
does not depend on it. This updates host packages, with a reboot only when
`/var/run/reboot-required` exists; it does not change service images, source,
saved configuration or Seed. Keep recoverable backups and provider-console access.

Supply private operator inputs: target hostname, administrative SSH port (2222
for [Public 7](#public-7-separate-administrative-and-gitlab-ssh)), key path and
independently verified host-key file; accepted clean remote tools checkout and
revision; persistence selector and expected mount/UUID; private receipt root;
and, optionally, the verifier's administrator `read_api` token-file selector.
Record the authorized package sources and reboot policy. Never put credentials
in the task text or public documentation.

Perform each run as follows; preserve receipts outside the source checkout:

1. Use SSH with `BatchMode=yes`, `IdentitiesOnly=yes`, `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`
   and the supplied `UserKnownHostsFile`, port and key. Verify the remote checkout,
   persistent mount/UUID and free space; record `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`,
   kernel, held packages and existing failed units. Defer on unexpected identity,
   storage, package-lock, `dpkg --audit` or unfinished platform-operation state.
2. From the remote accepted checkout, capture a new private baseline and run
   `bootstrapper/verify-runtime.py check` against it before changes. Use its
   [documented options](../bootstrapper/README.md#reviewed-replacement-host-initialization).
   Keep saved configuration/auth hashes and exact image identities unchanged.
   Refresh indexes with `sudo apt-get update`, then inspect
   `sudo apt-get -s --with-new-pkgs --no-remove upgrade`. Respect package holds
   and Ubuntu phasing; do not force phased updates, remove packages or upgrade
   the Ubuntu release. Docker/containerd, OpenSSH and firewall packages need
   particular review. If no upgrade or reboot is needed, report and finish.
3. Before any installation that can restart services, authenticate to Sync and
   inspect `/status`: require `needRestart`, `harvestInProgress`,
   `runnerSetupInProgress`, `defaultWizardSetupInProgress` and
   `projectOperationInProgress` explicitly false. Existing native operation leases,
   including environment leases, must be absent. Run the committed GitLab check:

   ```bash
   sudo docker exec -i system_gitlab_1 gitlab-rails runner - < gitlab/upgrade-preflight.rb
   ```

   Its JSON must show the accepted CE version, `runningJobs: 0` and
   `unfinishedBackgroundMigrations: 0`; exit zero alone is insufficient. If busy,
   leave jobs running and defer this maintenance without upgrades or reboot.
4. Reserve downtime against other operators; stop the owned public web proxy.
   In the existing GitLab container, use `gitlab-ctl stop` separately for `sshd`,
   `nginx`, `gitlab-workhorse`, `puma` and `sidekiq`; confirm they are down, then
   repeat the preflight before stopping databases. A raced job means resume the
   same GitLab services/proxy and defer with runners/controller untouched.
   Only after this final jobs-zero proof, stop the main runner pool through
   `docker exec -w /system/gitlab-runner system_bootstrapper_1 bash -e ./stop.sh main`,
   preserving registrations. Privately record the original controller/GitLab
   restart policies, then `docker update --restart=no system_bootstrapper_1 system_gitlab_1`
   so a package-triggered Docker restart cannot revive these writers
   ([restart-policy semantics](https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/start-containers-automatically/)). Stop the
   retained controller with `docker stop --time 30 system_bootstrapper_1`;
   wait for outstanding GitLab Docker execs to drain.
   Do not use top-level `stop.sh` or `bootstrapper/stop.sh`, which remove containers.
   Stop all GitLab services with `gitlab-ctl stop`, verify every runit service is
   down, then `docker stop --time 60 system_gitlab_1`; require exit zero and no OOM.
5. Install only the reviewed plan, keeping modified package configuration files:

   ```bash
   sudo env DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y --with-new-pkgs --no-remove \
     -o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold upgrade
   ```

   Recheck `dpkg --audit` and package-manager completion. Preserve Docker's mounted
   volume dependency, SSH socket overrides and firewall policy. Restore the exact
   recorded restart policies before authorized reboot or explicit container start.
   Reboot only if the marker exists. Otherwise start the retained GitLab/controller
   containers so native startup reconciles runners and routing. On failure, retain
   the stopped state and policy receipts for recovery; do not reboot blindly.
   Do not rebuild, restore Seed, patch code or change image selectors.
   See [APT upgrade options](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/noble/man8/apt-get.8.html)
   and [Ubuntu phasing](https://ubuntu.com/server/docs/explanation/software/about-apt-upgrade-and-phased-updates/).
6. If rebooted, wait for a fresh pinned SSH connection and a changed boot ID;
   require the original mount and automatic Docker/controller startup. In both
   reboot and no-reboot paths, run the
   native verifier against the original baseline, with `--timeout 1200` and the
   optional token file for fresh runner-contact proof. Check `dpkg --audit`, failed
   units, SSH/firewall and Docker bindings separately: administrative 2222 remains
   source-restricted, GitLab SSH 22 public, HTTP/HTTPS 80/443 unchanged and direct
   registry 5050 loopback. Record failures and deferred/phased packages accurately.

If cloud-init fails to find a primary interface during a rename, inspect the
journal, `ip -br link`, Netplan's actual `match`/`set-name` and udev properties.
Correct an incorrect network definition first. For a confirmed startup race,
verify the installed unit is `cloud-init-main.service` and systemd supports
`udevadm wait` before adding
`/etc/systemd/system/cloud-init-main.service.d/10-wait-for-primary-interface.conf`:

```ini
[Unit]
Wants=systemd-udev-trigger.service
After=systemd-udev-trigger.service
[Service]
ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/udevadm wait --timeout=30 --initialized=yes /sys/class/net/REPLACE_WITH_CONFIGURED_INTERFACE
```

Replace the interface selector with Netplan's configured final name, then reload
systemd and verify the next boot. This waits for that specific initialized device;
it does not add a global udev settle or justify `cloud-init clean` on an existing
installation. See [udevadm wait](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/udevadm.html).

To schedule the procedure, first test Codex authentication in a read-only run
and test pinned SSH from the actual cron account. The private task file should
reference this section and supply the inputs, authorization and failure policy.
Create its directory mode 0700 and inputs/reports mode 0600. Give each remote
run a new receipt directory and archive its result; `latest.md` is only a summary.
An optional **root user's crontab** entry below runs Sunday at 03:00 on a host
whose cron timezone is UTC. Substitute your absolute CLI, checkout and private
paths; verify the scheduler's timezone rather than assuming `TZ` changes cron.

```cron
0 3 * * 0 umask 077; /usr/bin/flock -n /private/maintenance/weekly.lock /usr/bin/timeout --kill-after=2m 90m /absolute/path/codex exec -C /path/to/reviewed/checkout --sandbox danger-full-access -c 'approval_policy="never"' --color never -o /private/maintenance/latest.md - < /private/maintenance/task.txt >> /private/maintenance/cron.log 2>&1
```

This explicitly grants unattended shell/network access: use only a trusted task,
checkout and host. The lock prevents overlapping cron runs; it is not a platform
lease. A timeout cannot prove a remote APT operation stopped: inspect its state
before recovery, never kill package managers or delete locks to force a retry.
Cron starts a separate agent run and saves local reports; it does not promise a
message in an existing chat. Check each run's time, exit result and log: an old
`latest.md` is not evidence of a new successful run. See the official
[Codex non-interactive documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/non-interactive-mode).

chapters.title: 6.1 Troubleshooting
chapters.markdown:
## 4. Troubleshooting

| Observation | Next step |
| --- | --- |
| `localhost` does not open | Keep an Ubuntu console open and check `sudo docker ps` |
| Connect reports Network Error | Check the address through Edit: `http://localhost/sync` at local first startup, then the configured Sync domain |
| Login is rejected | Retrieve the active values using the private local command in section 0.4; saved main settings override first-startup credentials |
| The form contains Example values | Connect and run Fetch first; an unconnected form is not the server configuration |
| Fetch returns 404 on a fresh instance | Reload the Wizard; both the Wizard and Sync must use versions supporting suggestions |
| Saved Example values return | Fetch prioritizes saved settings. Correct them explicitly in the Wizard; suggestions do not overwrite existing configuration |
| GitLab is not reachable yet | After Push triggers its automatic restart, wait for `healthy` and inspect GitLab logs if needed |
| Four configured runner containers appear as one GitLab runner | Open the runner detail page and inspect **Runner managers**; the shared pool has one entry with independent manager system IDs |
| Startup reports missing persistent storage | Check the selected mode and directory; mount an explicitly selected live volume instead of changing modes to bypass its guard |
| A pipeline waits for its runner after a GitLab restart | Register checks the pool and updates managed internal IP endpoints to the stable Docker service name |
| A pipeline cannot resolve `registry.localhost` | Run `sudo bash bootstrapper/prepare-local.sh` again in Ubuntu; WSL may reset local hosts entries at startup |
| `docker ps` shows no separate Sync Node container | Expected: Node runs inside the Bootstrapper container. `system_sync_1` is the NGINX access point at first startup |

See [Prepare-Host.md](../Prepare-Host.md) for further technical details.

chapters.title: 7. Recovery · retained live volume
chapters.markdown:
## Replace a host while retaining its data volume

This section is the explicit volume-backed reuse path. For fresh local working
storage populated from an external backup instead, use the
[configuration-plus-Seed restore procedure](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md#restore-an-external-seed-into-a-fresh-local-installation).
A default local installation does not preserve its working data when the VM is
deleted; Harvest to external storage and save matching configuration first.


This procedure reuses the current live data, including GitLab, configuration and
certificates. It does **not** restore an older Seed or upgrade the saved GitLab
version. Keep the volume when removing the old VM, and stop its writers cleanly
before detaching it when possible. Use the
[configuration-plus-Seed procedure](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md) instead when only a
completed Seed and configuration backup are available. A version change follows
the separate [evolution procedure](#5-evolving-a-running-system).

Before starting, obtain your accepted host-tools revision, recorded runtime
source/image identities, filesystem UUID, mount/data paths and complete saved
configuration. The recovery manifest and declared image archives must already
have been prepared through the
[image-recovery procedure](PERSISTENT_VOLUME.md#replacing-a-vm-while-retaining-live-data).
Choose enough host resources for GitLab and any simultaneous builds or disposable
tests. Keep the configured DNS names; update their A/AAAA records if the public
address changes. Public HTTPS requires ports 80 and 443 to reach this host. Do
not apply the local HTTP preparation from section 0.2 to this deployment.

1. On the replacement Ubuntu host, fetch source as in section 0.1. Select a
   reviewed tools revision containing the initialization entry point and initialize
   its exact submodules. A prepublished accepted source mirror or Git bundle
   containing the required commits can provide this checkout while the platform's
   own GitLab is unavailable:

   ```bash
   SYSTEM_TOOLS_REVISION=REPLACE_WITH_REVIEWED_TOOLS_COMMIT
   git checkout --detach "$SYSTEM_TOOLS_REVISION"
   git submodule update --init --recursive
   ```

   A plain source ZIP without Git history does not satisfy the initialization
   tool's commit/tree verification. Keep the checkout clean. The recorded
   controller source in the image manifest may be an earlier accepted revision;
   the tool checks its tree and Wizard
   gitlink separately and records the host-tools revision too. Do not update a
   submodule to its latest branch or change saved service versions to match the
   fresh-install examples.

2. Inspect `lsblk -f` and mount the **existing** filesystem at its previous
   absolute mount path. Replace these example assignments with your installation's
   values. Do not format the attached volume:

   ```bash
   PERSISTENCE_MODE=volume
   PERSISTENT_MOUNT=/mnt/bootstrapper-data
   PERSISTENT_DIR=/mnt/bootstrapper-data/platform
   SEED_DIR=/mnt/bootstrapper-data/seed
   PERSISTENT_UUID=REPLACE_WITH_EXISTING_UUID
   sudo install -d -m 0755 "$PERSISTENT_MOUNT"
   sudo mount "UUID=$PERSISTENT_UUID" "$PERSISTENT_MOUNT"
   findmnt --mountpoint "$PERSISTENT_MOUNT"
   ```

   If it is already mounted, verify its UUID and target instead of mounting it
   again. Recreate the private selector with only these storage settings; unrelated
   old image overrides could select the wrong services:

   ```bash
   sudo install -d -m 0700 /etc/system-bootstrapper
   sudo tee /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env >/dev/null <<EOF
   PERSISTENCE_MODE=volume
   PERSISTENT_MOUNT=$PERSISTENT_MOUNT
   PERSISTENT_DIR=$PERSISTENT_DIR
   SEED_DIR=$SEED_DIR
   PERSISTENT_UUID=$PERSISTENT_UUID
   EOF
   sudo chmod 0600 /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env
   ```

3. Verify that `platform/recovery/images.json` describes the recorded source,
   exact image IDs, local aliases and checksummed archives. The full manifest
   schema and input requirements are in the
   [initialization tool documentation](../bootstrapper/README.md). Missing source
   identities or aliases are a preparation failure, not permission to substitute
   a different image or copy a private recovery script onto the host.

4. If the retained configuration uses `GITLAB_SSH_BIND='22'`, first prepare and
   freshly test administration on port 2222 as described in
   [Public 7](#public-7-separate-administrative-and-gitlab-ssh), then free the host's
   port 22. A fresh Ubuntu host commonly reserves 22 for its own SSH service;
   the initializer will not move that listener for you. Perform the host/firewall
   steps before initialization and let the initializer start GitLab; the
   in-controller reconciliation commands in Public 7 are for an already running
   installation. Preserve the retained GitLab binding instead of reverting saved
   configuration to a first-install example.

   Run the committed initialization coordinator from this reviewed checkout:

   ```bash
   sudo env PERSISTENCE_ENV_FILE=/etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env \
     bash bootstrapper/initialize.sh \
       --install-host \
       --receipt-dir /var/log/system-bootstrapper/initialize-REPLACE_WITH_OPERATION_ID \
       --timeout 1200
   ```

   Choose a new receipt directory for each attempt. `--install-host` installs the
   documented Ubuntu dependencies, Docker and Certbot. Omit it if the host is
   already prepared. The coordinator validates storage, source and archives,
   captures a baseline, loads the declared images, installs volume/TLS host
   integration, starts the services and checks their actual application readiness.
   It never formats a filesystem, restores Seed or changes the saved configuration.

   For a small host with sufficient **root-disk** space, explicitly add
   `--swap-gib 8` if you want the tool to create swap. It refuses an existing
   `/swapfile` or insufficient free space; swap does not replace RAM needed for
   simultaneous candidate tests. Add `--renewal-dry-run` on a retained public
   HTTPS installation to test Certbot through the shared renewal lease without
   stopping the proxy. Add `--redirect-from https://example.com` only when that
   origin is configured to redirect to the public Wizard.

   For fresh GitLab runner-manager contact verification, provide
   `--gitlab-token-file /root/REPLACE_WITH_PRIVATE_API_TOKEN_FILE`. The file must
   be private (mode 0600) and contain a token with the documented administrator
   `read_api` access. It is not a command-line token value. Without that input,
   the receipt marks the API contact check as skipped; running containers alone
   must not be reported as proof that managers are online.

5. Inspect the private operation status and structured verification receipt. The
   checks cover unchanged saved configuration, exact service images and Cube,
   persistent mount backing, authenticated Sync Fetch, Wizard/GitLab/registry
   routing and configured host TLS integration. Missing private Wizard images
   are pulled at the saved immutable digest through
   [temporary scoped registry recovery](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md#pulling-a-restored-private-wizard-image).
   Do not publish the private configuration, token file or raw logs.

   To repeat runtime verification against the captured baseline, use the same
   committed verifier and add the optional token/redirect arguments as needed:

   ```bash
   sudo python3 bootstrapper/verify-runtime.py check \
     --persistence-env /etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env \
     --baseline /var/log/system-bootstrapper/initialize-REPLACE_WITH_OPERATION_ID/baseline.json \
     --output /var/log/system-bootstrapper/initialize-REPLACE_WITH_OPERATION_ID/recheck.json \
     --timeout 1200
   ```

If a required entry point fails because behavior is missing, fix that behavior
through a merge request and its applicable checks before deploying the corrected
tools. Keep incomplete-operation markers and receipts for diagnosis; do not
bypass guards or restore a stale Seed to make a host replacement continue.

chapters.title: 7.1 Working data and independent backups
chapters.markdown:
# Working data and independent Seed backups

The platform has two storage roles:

| Role | Purpose | Availability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Live working data (`PERSISTENT_DIR`) | GitLab/database/registry data, configuration, certificates and runner state. | Required while the platform runs. |
| Seed backup (`SEED_DIR`) | Verified cold snapshots created by Harvest and read during explicit restore. | Required only for Harvest or restore. |

A fresh Ubuntu/WSL installation uses its own system disk for live data. An
external disk, USB stick or cloud volume is not a prerequisite. Keeping a Seed
on separate media permits recovery after losing that system disk. Configuration
backup remains a separate Wizard export, and source/images remain declared
recovery inputs. A Seed is not a continuously synchronized database copy.

## Paths and selectors

With no storage selector, a fresh installation uses:

```sh
PERSISTENCE_MODE=local
PERSISTENT_MOUNT=/
PERSISTENT_DIR=/var/lib/system-bootstrapper/platform
```

The optional root-owned file `/etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env` selects a
custom layout. Use Linux storage under WSL, not a Windows-mounted directory such
as `/mnt/c`. The local preflight checks canonical paths, permissions, writable
space and required Unix filesystem behavior. Protect the file with mode 0600.

For live data on an attached filesystem, opt in explicitly:

```sh
PERSISTENCE_MODE=volume
PERSISTENT_MOUNT=/mnt/bootstrapper-data
PERSISTENT_DIR=/mnt/bootstrapper-data/platform
PERSISTENT_UUID=REPLACE_WITH_EXISTING_FILESYSTEM_UUID
```

An existing selector with `PERSISTENT_MOUNT` and no mode keeps the legacy volume
contract. A missing or mismatched selected live volume stops startup; there is
no fallback to a new directory on the root disk. Neither changing the mode nor
editing a path migrates existing data. Stop writers and make a deliberate,
verified copy before changing layouts. Existing Docker volume metadata also
needs deliberate reconciliation when a selected bind destination changes.

## Select backup media independently

Add the backup destination to the same private selector when needed:

```sh
SEED_MOUNT=/media/bootstrapper-backup
SEED_DIR=/media/bootstrapper-backup/seed
SEED_UUID=REPLACE_WITH_BACKUP_FILESYSTEM_UUID
```

Mount that existing filesystem deliberately and create its `seed` directory
before Harvest or restore. `SEED_MOUNT` requires the intended mounted target;
an absent mount is an error, not permission to create a lookalike root-disk
backup directory. `SEED_UUID` adds an identity check. A local-mode installation requires an explicitly mounted external Seed target
on a different filesystem. This prevents backing the only recovery copy onto
the VM disk that it must recover. Legacy volume-backed installations may retain
a disjoint Seed directory on that same explicitly selected live volume; losing
that volume still loses both copies.

Live and Seed roots must be canonical, disjoint paths. Neither may contain the
other. Escaping symlinks, overlapping roots and unexpected nested mounts are
rejected. Live data and Seed may be on different filesystems. Their storage
checks are independent: an unavailable backup target must not block ordinary
startup, Docker lifecycle, configuration Fetch/Push or certificate renewal.

The controller and GitLab do not retain `/seed` mounts. An explicit operation
starts a temporary helper from the exact controller image, validates the host
paths/mount identity and binds backup storage for that operation only. Harvest
checks the target and available space before stopping GitLab. A shared lease in
the live configuration directory serializes operations even if a different
backup destination is selected, and a second lease excludes certificate renewal.
Detach backup media only after the operation and its helper have completed.

## Live directory layout

The layout below is relative to `PERSISTENT_DIR` in either mode:

```text
platform/
├── configuration/        # Main settings, project receipts and Sync auth
├── wizard-public/        # Derived public operator/privacy details only
├── gitlab/
│   ├── config/           # GitLab secrets and service configuration
│   ├── logs/
│   └── data/             # Repositories, database, registry and artifacts
├── ssl/                  # Served certificates and HTTP-01 webroot
├── templates/            # Proxy and managed environment fragments
├── synctemplates/
├── runners/
│   └── <pool>/<index>/
│       ├── config/       # Runner auth and stable manager system ID
│       └── home/
└── host/
    └── letsencrypt/      # Full Certbot account/archive/live/renewal tree
```

Optional `recovery/` material may hold image archives and a recovery manifest.
Source can be fetched freshly; it is not required live service state. Preserve
numeric ownership, modes and symlinks when copying service data, and protect
configuration, credentials and certificate keys with restrictive permissions.

Compose named data volumes use explicit local-driver bind destinations beneath
`PERSISTENT_DIR`; runner managers bind their own directories. Inspect the actual
sources and filesystem rather than trusting volume names. The controller mounts
configuration at `/state` and uses `SYSTEM_CONFIG_DIR=/state`; compatibility
links make shell scripts and Sync read the same saved settings and receipts.
Attached settings take precedence over files baked into an image.

Each runner manager retains a separate system ID while sharing its pool's
GitLab runner record. Scaling down retains its directories for reuse. Caches and
workspaces can be recreated and are not configuration-plus-Seed recovery inputs.

The controller derives only the six public Website settings into
`wizard-public/privacy-instance.json`; the Wizard mounts that directory
read-only. Private configuration, Sync credentials and GitLab tokens are never
copied there. Missing public settings use marked examples; saved empty values
remain empty. The file can be regenerated from configuration.

## Certificates and host integration

Persist the full Certbot tree beneath `host/letsencrypt`: account keys,
`archive`, `live`, renewal configuration and hooks. `live` symlinks alone are
insufficient. Install Certbot separately, then run
`sudo bash bootstrapper/install-volume-host.sh` from the selected checkout.
The compatibility-named installer handles both live storage modes. Volume mode
retains its fstab/Docker mount dependency; local mode adds no external-storage
prerequisite. Neither mode adds a dependency on removable Seed media.

Host integration connects `/etc/letsencrypt` to retained live state, installs the
certificate deploy hook and renewal lease, and rebinds webroot paths to
`PERSISTENT_DIR/ssl/acme-http01`. NGINX serves that directory at `/ssl/acme-http01`.
Conflicting active Certbot state on host and live storage must be reconciled.
The installer enables `certbot.timer` when available. After NGINX is reachable:

```sh
sudo system-certbot renew --dry-run
```

Use this wrapper for manual renewal too. Do not modify certificate state through
unmanaged Certbot processes while Harvest or restore is active.

## Replace a host from an external Seed

Keep a completed Seed, its matching separate Wizard configuration backup and
the recorded source/image inputs before deleting a machine with local live
data. Deleting that machine deletes the local working data. Attaching an older
backup does not make it a snapshot of later changes.

Follow [configuration-plus-Seed recovery](RECOVERY_CONTRACT.md) on the new host:
select a fresh local directory, attach the backup target, validate and restore
the completed Seed before starting writers, then start services. The original
live directories are not recovery inputs. After successful restore and
verification, remove the transient helper and detach the backup medium; normal
operation and TLS renewal continue from the new local live data.

Keeping an already populated live volume and reattaching it is a separate
convenience path, described below. It does not prove external-Seed recovery.

## Replacing a VM while retaining live data

1. Stop writers cleanly before detaching storage. Retain the volume explicitly
   when deleting the VM; do not format it or initialize another filesystem over it.
2. Provision a compatible Ubuntu host, attach the volume and mount its existing
   filesystem. Fetch the intended System revision with pinned submodules. Install
   Docker using `sudo bash bootstrapper/install.sh`; install Certbot separately.
3. Recreate `/etc/system-bootstrapper/persistence.env` with
   `PERSISTENCE_MODE=volume` and the retained mount/directory/UUID selectors.
   Check mount/UUID and saved configuration. Run the host integration described
   above. Do not apply an older Seed over the retained live data.
4. Make exact required image references available. Rebuild custom controller
   images from the intended source, pull public images at recorded versions or
   digests, and retain immutable private Wizard pins. Optional managed Review/Beta
   helpers require their own clean rebuild and explicit reprovisioning if their
   prior local image is absent; see the [managed environment guide](../project-bootstrap/wizard-environments/README.md).
5. Run `sudo bash start.sh` from that checkout. It checks storage, builds the
   controller and starts services using retained configuration. Container IPs,
   networks and proxy configuration are regenerated. Change DNS if the host's
   address changed while preserving the configured domain names.
6. Verify Wizard/Sync, GitLab, registry authentication, runner managers and TLS
   renewal. Inspect every retained mount and named-volume device against the
   attached filesystem.

An alternative archive-based path is `bootstrapper/recover-volume.sh`. It requires
operator-prepared `PERSISTENT_DIR/recovery/images.json`, the referenced gzip image
archives with SHA-256 values, public image references and a retained selector file;
these private recovery artifacts are not supplied by a source checkout. Set
`PERSISTENCE_ENV_FILE` to that selector and invoke the script from the intended
checkout. `--verify` checks storage and archive checksums without starting services.
Without that flag it loads archives, pulls missing public references, installs
host integration and starts without rebuilding. Never treat an unavailable local
tag or an undeclared archive as a recovery guarantee.

### Preparing the optional image archives

Prepare these inputs deliberately on a host where the intended images are
available, before relying on archive-based replacement. Create a private
`PERSISTENT_DIR/recovery/images/` directory. For each custom image, stream
`docker image save <recorded-image-reference> | gzip` into a file in that
directory, check that both commands succeed, then record the compressed file's
`sha256sum`. Keep the original image tag in the archive, or explicitly tag the
image with the selector that the saved main configuration uses before saving.
For immutable helper image IDs, preserve the exact original image content.

Write `PERSISTENT_DIR/recovery/images.json` with these two lists. Replace the
placeholders with the archive's actual checksum and public image references:

```json
{
  "archives": [
    {
      "file": "images/controller.tar.gz",
      "sha256": "<64 hexadecimal characters from sha256sum>"
    }
  ],
  "publicImages": [
    {
      "reference": "nginx@sha256:<recorded digest>",
      "tag": "nginx:retained"
    }
  ]
}
```

Include every required custom archive and public GitLab, Runner and proxy image,
using references compatible with the retained installation. Each public entry is
pulled if absent and given its declared local alias; this does not change the
saved configuration. Ensure its selected reference or alias matches that
configuration. The private Wizard image can remain an exact registry digest and
be recovered from the retained registry during startup. Protect the manifest and
archives, retain an independent record of their expected checksums and verify
them with `recover-volume.sh --verify` before startup. Image archives do not
replace the live filesystem, complete saved configuration or Certbot state.

Before deliberately moving live data between local and volume layouts, stop
writers, copy data consistently and retain a rollback copy. Changing a selector
does not copy or migrate data. Recreate Docker volume metadata only
after verifying its exact identity and destination. Do not delete unrelated
volumes or run a global Docker prune.
